Order matter karta hai stylistically nahi lekin dono chahiye. 12-16. Standard reversal plus counter. 17. group_prev.next = prev — prev reversed group ka naya head. 18. group_start.next = current — current group ke baad wala node (ya None). Yeh line 6.3 mein nahi thi kyunki wahan prev = group_next trick ne yeh kaam kar diya tha. 19. group_prev = group_start — reversal ke baad group_start tail hai, toh wahi ab "processed hisse ka aakhri node" hai. 20-23. Skip phase. k steps traverse, bina kuch badle. - Line 21 ka check zaroori hai warna None.next par crash. - return dummy.next — list khatam ho gayi, kaam poora. 24. return dummy.next.

    Kyun prev = None yahan safe hai lekin 6.3 mein trick use ki thi: 6.3 mein group hamesha exactly k ka hota tha (partial ko chhod dete the), toh group_next pehle se pata tha. Yahan group partial ho sakta hai, toh group_next reversal ke baad hi pata chalta hai (current ke roop mein). Isliye explicit reconnection.

    Dry run — 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8, k = 2 (A..H)

    Setup: dummy -> A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> F -> G -> H. group_prev = dummy.

    Round 1 — reverse A, B:

    prev = None, current = A, group_start = A, count = 0.

    Iter current prev count next_node Assignment prev after current after count after
    1 A None 0 B A.next = None A B 1
    2 B A 1 C B.next = A B C 2
    3 — — 2 — count < 2 False → exit — — —

    Line 17: dummy.next = B. Line 18: A.next = C. State: dummy -> B -> A -> C -> D -> E -> F -> G -> H.

    Skip phase: group_prev = A. 2 steps: A -> C, C -> D. group_prev = D.

    Round 2 — reverse E, F:

    current = D.next = E, group_start = E, prev = None.

    Iter current prev count next_node Assignment prev after current after
    1 E None 0 F E.next = None E F
    2 F E 1 G F.next = E F G
    3 — — 2 — exit — —

    Line 17: D.next = F. Line 18: E.next = G. State: dummy -> B -> A -> C -> D -> F -> E -> G -> H.

    Skip phase: group_prev = E. 2 steps: E -> G, G -> H. group_prev = H.

    Round 3: Line 6: H.next is None → loop exit → return dummy.next = B.

    Final: 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 6 -> 5 -> 7 -> 8. Expected se match.

    Dry run — 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 2 (A..E)

    Round 1: reverse A,B → dummy -> B -> A -> C -> D -> E. Skip 2: group_prev = A → C → D. Round 2: current = D.next = E, group_start = E.

    Iter current prev count next_node Assignment prev current
    1 E None 0 None E.next = None E None
    2 — — 1 — current is not None False → exit — —

    Line 11 ka pehla condition trigger hua — sirf ek node bacha tha. Line 17: D.next = E. Line 18: E.next = None. State: dummy -> B -> A -> C -> D -> E.

    Skip phase: group_prev = E. Loop iteration 1: E.next is None → return dummy.next = B.

    Final: 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5. Sahi — akela 5 reverse hua (jo no-op hai) aur waise ka waisa raha.

    Complexity

    • Time: O(n). Har node exactly ek baar visit hota hai — ya reverse phase mein ya skip phase mein. 6.3 se better (wahan 2n tha) kyunki yahan pre-counting nahi hai.
    • Space: O(1).

    Edge cases

    Case Input k Output Kyun
    k = 1 1->2->3 1 1->2->3 Guard
    List exactly k 1->2 2 2->1 Ek reverse, phir skip par exit
    List = 2k 1->2->3->4 2 2->1->3->4 Reverse, skip, exit
    Partial in reverse phase 1->2->3->4->5 2 2->1->3->4->5 Upar
    Partial in skip phase 1->2->3 2 2->1->3 Skip loop None par exit
    Empty None 2 None Guard
    Single 1 2 1 Reverse (no-op), skip exit
    k >= n 1->2->3 5 3->2->1 Poori list ek group

    Variations

    • Skip pehle, phir reverse — phase order swap; ek boolean flag se dono handle karo.
    • Alag reverse aur skip sizes — reverse_k aur skip_m do parameters.
    • Partial group ko reverse mat karo — 6.3 wala pre-counting laga do.
    • Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups (2074) — group sizes badhte jaate hain.
    • Har alternate group ko kuch aur karo (jaise sort) — same skeleton, alag operation.

    Interview answer: "This is the k-group reversal with a skip phase alternating in. Each iteration of the outer loop does two things: reverse the next k nodes, then walk forward k nodes without touching anything.

    One difference from the plain k-group version. There I checked upfront whether a full group of k existed and left a short tail untouched. Here a short tail still gets reversed if it lands in a reverse phase, so instead of pre-counting I bound the reversal loop by both a counter and a null check — whichever hits first.

    That also changes how I reconnect. In the plain version I could seed the reversal's prev pointer with the node after the group, which made the tail reconnection free. That trick needs to know where the group ends before reversing, which I don't here. So I save the group's first node — which becomes its tail — and after reversing I explicitly point it at wherever the reversal stopped.

    The skip phase then just advances the group-predecessor pointer k times, bailing out if it runs off the end.

    Every node is visited exactly once, so O(n) time — actually slightly better than the k-group version, which touches each node twice because of its counting pass. O(1) space. And a dummy node in front keeps the first group, which changes the head, from needing a special case."

    Problem 6.5 — Rotate A Linked List¶

    Problem statement

    Linked list ko right ki taraf k places rotate karo.

    Input:  1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 2
Output: 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3
        (aakhri 2 nodes shuru mein aa gaye)

Input:  0 -> 1 -> 2, k = 4
Output: 2 -> 0 -> 1
        (k = 4, length = 3, toh effectively k = 1)

Input:  1 -> 2, k = 0
Output: 1 -> 2

    Pehla instinct — brute force

    k baar "aakhri node ko aage laao" karo.

    def rotate_brute(head, k):
    if head is None or head.next is None:         # 1: 0 ya 1 node
        return head                               # 2
    for _ in range(k):                            # 3: k baar rotate
        prev = None                               # 4: aakhri se pehle wala
        current = head                            # 5
        while current.next:                       # 6: tail dhoondo
            prev = current                        # 7
            current = current.next                # 8
        # ab current = tail, prev = second last
        prev.next = None                          # 9: tail ko list se kaato
        current.next = head                       # 10: tail ko aage lagao
        head = current                            # 11: naya head
    return head                                   # 12

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. Guard. 3. for _ in range(k): — k baar poori traversal. Yehi problem hai. 4-8. Har baar tail dhoondhna — O(n). 9-11. Tail ko detach karke front mein lagao. 12. Return.

    Complexity: Time O(n * k). Agar k = 10^9 (jo constraint allow karta hai) toh yeh kabhi khatam nahi hoga. Space O(1).

    Isme problem kya hai

    k bahut bada ho sakta hai. Aur k = n par list wapas original ban jaati hai — matlab hum wahi kaam baar baar kar rahe hain.

    The insight

    Do observations, dono zaroori:

    1. k ko n se modulo kar do. n rotations = koi rotation nahi. Toh k = k % n se k hamesha 0 se n-1 ke beech aa jaata hai. k = 10^9, n = 5 → k = 10^9 % 5. Yeh ek line poora O(n*k) se O(n) bana deti hai.

    2. Rotation ek "cut and reattach" hai, node-by-node movement nahi. Right by k rotate karne ka matlab: naya head position n - k par hai (0-indexed). Toh:

    3. List ko circular bana do (tail ko head se jodo),
    4. n - k steps chalo,
    5. wahan se list ko kaat do.

    Circular banane wala trick isliye accha hai ki traversal ek hi baar hoti hai aur koi "wrap around" logic nahi likhna padta.

    Optimal solution

    def rotate_right(head, k):
    if head is None or head.next is None or k == 0:   # 1: kuch nahi badlega
        return head                               # 2

    # STEP 1: length ginno aur tail dhoondo
    n = 1                                         # 3: head ko already gin liya
    tail = head                                   # 4
    while tail.next is not None:                  # 5: aakhri node tak
        tail = tail.next                          # 6
        n += 1                                    # 7

    # STEP 2: k ko normalise karo
    k = k % n                                     # 8: n rotations = zero rotations
    if k == 0:                                    # 9: poora chakkar -> kuch nahi badla
        return head                               # 10

    # STEP 3: list ko circular banao
    tail.next = head                              # 11: ab yeh ek ring hai

    # STEP 4: naye tail tak chalo aur kaato
    steps_to_new_tail = n - k                     # 12: naya tail is position par (1-indexed count)
    new_tail = head                               # 13
    for _ in range(steps_to_new_tail - 1):        # 14: -1 kyunki head par already khade hain
        new_tail = new_tail.next                  # 15
    new_head = new_tail.next                      # 16: naya head uske turant baad
    new_tail.next = None                          # 17: ring todo -- ZAROORI
    return new_head                               # 18

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. Guards. k == 0 bhi guard mein hai — chhota optimisation. 3. n = 1 — 0 se nahi, 1 se. Kyunki tail already head par hai, yaani ek node gin liya. Loop sirf baaki gine ga. n = 0 likhne se off-by-one. 4. tail = head. 5-7. while tail.next is not None: — tail.next check kar rahe hain, tail nahi. while tail: likhte toh loop ke baad tail None ho jaata aur line 11 crash karti. Humein aakhri node chahiye, uske aage wala None nahi. 8. k = k % n — yeh ek line hi O(n*k) ko O(n) banati hai. 9-10. k == 0 after modulo → list waisi hi rahegi. Yeh check na ho toh line 12 mein steps_to_new_tail = n, line 14 range(n-1) — jo actually sahi answer hi deta hai. Toh yeh guard optional hai, bas fast path hai. 11. tail.next = head — circular bana diya. Ab is point ke baad koi bhi traversal infinite ho sakti hai, isliye line 17 tak careful rehna hai. 12. steps_to_new_tail = n - k — kyun n - k? Right by k rotate karne ka matlab hai ki aakhri k nodes aage aa jaayenge. Toh naya head original list ka (n - k + 1)-th node hai (1-indexed), aur naya tail (n - k)-th node. Check: n = 5, k = 2 → steps = 3 → naya tail 3rd node (value 3), naya head 4th node (value 4). Output 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3. Sahi. 13. new_tail = head — position 1 par. 14. for _ in range(steps_to_new_tail - 1): — -1 isliye ki head position 1 hai, aur humein position n-k tak jaana hai, toh n-k-1 steps. Check: steps = 3 → range(2) → 2 steps → position 3. Sahi. Yeh sabse common off-by-one hai. range(steps) likhne se ek node aage nikal jaate ho. 15. new_tail = new_tail.next. 16. new_head = new_tail.next — line 17 se pehle save karna zaroori hai, kyunki line 17 use None kar degi. 17. new_tail.next = None — ring todo. Yeh bhoolna sabse mehnga bug hai — list circular reh jaati hai aur koi bhi traversal hang kar jaati hai. 18. return new_head.

    Dry run — 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 2 (A..E)

    Step 1: tail = A, n = 1.

    Iter tail tail.next? tail after n after
    1 A B B 2
    2 B C C 3
    3 C D D 4
    4 D E E 5
    5 E None → exit E 5

    n = 5, tail = E.

    Step 2: k = 2 % 5 = 2. Not zero. Step 3: E.next = A → ring A->B->C->D->E->A. Step 4: steps_to_new_tail = 5 - 2 = 3. new_tail = A. range(3 - 1) = range(2):

    Iter new_tail before new_tail after
    1 A B
    2 B C

    new_tail = C. new_head = C.next = D. C.next = None.

    Final: D(4) -> E(5) -> A(1) -> B(2) -> C(3) = 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3. Sahi.

    Dry run — 0 -> 1 -> 2, k = 4 (A,B,C) — modulo test

    Step 1: n = 3, tail = C. Step 2: k = 4 % 3 = 1. Step 3: C.next = A. Step 4: steps = 3 - 1 = 2. range(1) → 1 step → new_tail = B. new_head = B.next = C. B.next = None.

    Final: C(2) -> A(0) -> B(1) = 2 -> 0 -> 1. Sahi.

    Bina modulo ke: steps = 3 - 4 = -1, range(-2) khaali → new_tail = A, new_head = B, output 1 -> 2 -> 0 — galat. Yeh dikhata hai ki line 8 optional nahi hai.

    Complexity

    • Time: O(n). Ek pass length ke liye, ek partial pass cut point ke liye. Total at most 2n.
    • Space: O(1).

    Edge cases

    Case Input k Output Kyun
    k = 0 1->2->3 0 1->2->3 Guard
    k = n 1->2->3 3 1->2->3 Modulo → 0
    k = n + 1 1->2->3 4 3->1->2 Modulo → 1
    k huge 1->2 10^9 depends on parity Modulo
    Single node 1 5 1 Guard
    Empty None 3 None Guard
    Two nodes 1->2 1 2->1
    k = n - 1 1->2->3 2 2->3->1

    Variations

    • Rotate left by k — k_right = n - (k % n), ya seedha steps_to_new_tail = k % n.
    • Rotate array by k (LeetCode 189) — teen reversals wala trick: poora reverse, phir pehle k reverse, phir baaki reverse.
    • Split list in parts (725) — same length-then-cut skill.
    • Rotate karo bina length ginne — possible nahi, kyunki k % n ke liye n chahiye.
    • Circular linked list mein rotate — aur bhi simple, bas head pointer sarka do.

    Interview answer: "Two things make this efficient. First, k can be far larger than the list length, and rotating by n leaves the list unchanged — so I reduce k modulo n immediately. Without that, k of a billion means a billion rotations.

    Second, a rotation isn't a sequence of moves, it's a single cut and reattach. Rotating right by k means the last k nodes move to the front, so the new head is at position n minus k plus one and the new tail is the node just before it.

    So: walk once to find the length and the tail, reduce k, join the tail to the head to make it circular, then walk n minus k minus one steps from the head to land on the new tail. Save its next as the new head, then break the ring by nulling the new tail's next.

    The circular step is what removes all the wrap-around bookkeeping — after joining, finding the cut point is just counting forward.

    Three details I'd watch. When counting the length I loop on tail.next, not tail, because I need the last node itself, not the null past it. The walk is n minus k minus one steps, not n minus k, because I start already standing on the head. And breaking the ring is not optional — forget it and every later traversal hangs.

    O(n) time, O(1) space."

    Problem 6.6 — Swap Nodes In Pairs¶

    Problem statement

    Har do consecutive nodes ko aapas mein swap karo. Values swap nahi karni — actual nodes swap karne hain.

    Input:  1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4
Output: 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3

Input:  1 -> 2 -> 3
Output: 2 -> 1 -> 3      (akela 3 waisa hi)

Input:  1
Output: 1

    Pehla instinct — brute force

    Values swap kar do.

    def swap_pairs_brute(head):
    current = head                                # 1
    while current is not None and current.next is not None:   # 2: pair bacha hai?
        current.val, current.next.val = current.next.val, current.val   # 3: VALUE swap
        current = current.next.next               # 4: do aage
    return head                                   # 5

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1. current = head.
    2. while current is not None and current.next is not None: — pair ke liye do nodes chahiye. Short-circuit order zaroori hai.
    3. current.val, current.next.val = current.next.val, current.val — Python tuple swap, values ke liye.
    4. current = current.next.next — do steps, kyunki ek pair process ho gaya.
    5. return head — head node same rehta hai (sirf uski value badli).

    Complexity: Time O(n), Space O(1). Technically efficient hai!

    Isme problem kya hai

    Efficiency mein kuch galat nahi hai — problem statement mein hai. Problem explicitly kehti hai "nodes swap karo, values nahi." Aur yeh reasonable requirement hai: agar node mein bade objects hon toh value copy mehngi hai, aur agar koi aur code purane node references pakde baitha ho toh unke liye data silently badal jaayega.

    Yeh ek acha interview moment hai — brute force dikhao, phir khud bolo "but the problem asks for node swaps, so here's that version."

    The insight

    Yeh Problem 6.3 ka k = 2 case hai. Lekin k = 2 par pointer manipulation ko explicitly likhna zyada saaf hai (general k-group code isse zyada bhaari hai).

    Har pair (a, b) ke liye teen links badalne hain: 1. prev.next = b — pichhle hisse ko b se jodo. 2. a.next = b.next — a ko pair ke aage wale se jodo. 3. b.next = a — b ko a se jodo.

    Order matter karta hai — b.next ko a par lagane se pehle b.next ki purani value (a.next mein) save honi chahiye. Isliye step 2 step 3 se pehle.

    Aur head badalta hai, toh dummy node chahiye.

    Optimal solution

    def swap_pairs(head):
    dummy = ListNode(0)                           # 1: head badalne wala hai
    dummy.next = head                             # 2
    prev = dummy                                  # 3: current pair se pehle wala node

    while prev.next is not None and prev.next.next is not None:   # 4: poora pair bacha hai?
        first = prev.next                         # 5: pair ka pehla node
        second = prev.next.next                   # 6: pair ka dusra node

        first.next = second.next                  # 7: first ko pair ke AAGE wale se jodo
        second.next = first                       # 8: second ko first se jodo (swap)
        prev.next = second                        # 9: pichhla hissa second se jodo

        prev = first                              # 10: first ab pair ka TAIL hai -> naya prev
    return dummy.next                             # 11

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. Dummy. 1 -> 2 par head 2 ban jaata hai, toh dummy ke bina if conditions likhni padti. 3. prev = dummy — hamesha "current pair se pehle wala node". 4. while prev.next is not None and prev.next.next is not None: — do nodes chahiye ek pair ke liye. Agar sirf ek bacha hai toh loop ruk jaata hai aur woh node waisa ka waisa rehta hai — exactly jo problem maangti hai. Short-circuit: prev.next None hone par prev.next.next evaluate nahi hoga. 5-6. first aur second — naam dene se code padhne layak ban jaata hai. prev.next.next.next type chains likhna bug ka invitation hai. 7. first.next = second.next — yeh line 8 se PEHLE honi chahiye. Line 8 second.next ko overwrite kar degi. Agar order ulta karein toh first.next = first ho jaata → self loop. 8. second.next = first — asli swap. 9. prev.next = second — yeh line 7 aur 8 ke baad bhi ho sakti hai ya pehle bhi (kyunki first aur second local variables mein saved hain), lekin baad mein likhna zyada logical lagta hai: "pehle pair ke andar ka kaam, phir bahar se connection." 10. prev = first — swap ke baad first pair ka aakhri node hai (kyunki order ab second -> first hai). Toh agle pair ke liye wahi prev hai. prev = prev.next.next likhna bhi kaam karta lekin prev = first clearer hai. 11. return dummy.next — naya head. return head galat hoga (woh ab dusra node hai).

    Recursive version (bahut chhota aur interview mein pasand kiya jaata hai):

    def swap_pairs_recursive(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:         # 12: 0 ya 1 node -> kuch nahi
        return head                               # 13
    second = head.next                            # 14: pair ka dusra node -- naya head banega
    head.next = swap_pairs_recursive(second.next) # 15: baaki list ko recursively swap karke jodo
    second.next = head                            # 16: swap complete
    return second                                 # 17: second ab pair ka head hai

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    12-13. Base cases. head.next is None odd-length list ka aakhri node handle karta hai. 14. second = head.next — save karo, kyunki line 15 head.next badal degi. 15. head.next = swap_pairs_recursive(second.next) — recursion par bharosa. second.next se aage ki poori list swap ho kar aayegi, aur head (jo ab pair ka tail hai) us se judega. 16. second.next = head — pair ke andar ka swap. 17. return second.

    Trade-off: O(n) stack space, aur 1000+ nodes par RecursionError.

    Dry run — iterative — 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 (A,B,C,D)

    Setup: dummy -> A -> B -> C -> D. prev = dummy.

    Round 1:

    Line 4: dummy.next = A (not None), dummy.next.next = B (not None) → enter. Line 5-6: first = A, second = B. Line 7: A.next = B.next = C. Line 8: B.next = A. Line 9: dummy.next = B. Line 10: prev = A.

    State: dummy -> B -> A -> C -> D.

    Link Before round 1 After round 1
    dummy.next A B
    A.next B C
    B.next C A
    C.next D D

    Round 2:

    Line 4: A.next = C, A.next.next = D → enter. Line 5-6: first = C, second = D. Line 7: C.next = D.next = None. Line 8: D.next = C. Line 9: A.next = D. Line 10: prev = C.

    State: dummy -> B -> A -> D -> C -> None.

    Round 3:

    Line 4: C.next is None → exit.

    Line 11: return dummy.next = B.

    Final: 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3. Sahi.

    Dry run — 1 -> 2 -> 3 (A,B,C) — odd length

    Round 1: first = A, second = B. A.next = C, B.next = A, dummy.next = B, prev = A. State: dummy -> B -> A -> C.

    Round 2: A.next = C (not None), A.next.next = C.next = None → condition fail, exit.

    Return B. Final: 2 -> 1 -> 3. C untouched. Sahi.

    Dry run — recursive — 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4

    Call head second Recurse on Returns Assignments
    swap(A) A B B.next = C (pending) —
    swap(C) C D D.next = None (pending) —
    swap(None) None — — None base case
    back in swap(C) C D — D C.next = None, D.next = C
    back in swap(A) A B — B A.next = D, B.next = A

    Final: B -> A -> D -> C. Sahi.

    Complexity

    Iterative: - Time: O(n). Har node ek baar. - Space: O(1).

    Recursive: - Time: O(n). - Space: O(n) stack.

    Edge cases

    Case Input Output Kyun
    Empty None None Line 4 pehla check
    Single 1 1 prev.next.next None
    Two 1->2 2->1 Ek round
    Three 1->2->3 2->1->3 Upar
    Four 1->2->3->4 2->1->4->3 Upar
    Same values 1->1->1->1 1->1->1->1 Structure badla, dikhta same
    Long even 10^5 nodes swapped Iterative fine
    Long odd 10^5+1 last unchanged

    Variations

    • Swap in groups of k — Problem 6.3 (k = 2 yahan ka special case hai).
    • Swap nodes at position k from start and end (LeetCode 1721) — wahan values swap karna acceptable hai, alag problem.
    • Odd Even Linked List (328) — nodes ko odd/even index ke hisaab se separate karo.
    • Recursive version — upar.
    • Doubly linked list mein swap — prev pointers bhi update karne hain, double kaam.

    Interview answer: "The one-line version swaps the values, which is O(n) time and O(1) space and passes most tests. But the problem specifically says to swap the nodes, and that distinction matters in practice: if the nodes carry large payloads, copying values is expensive, and if anything else holds a reference to a node, its data silently changes underneath it. So I'd show the value swap, name it as not meeting the requirement, and then write the pointer version.

    For the pointer version I keep a pointer to the node before the current pair. For each pair, three links change: the first node points past the pair, the second points back at the first, and the predecessor points at the second.

    The order matters — I have to redirect the first node before the second points at it, because that assignment overwrites the second's next. Reversing those two lines gives a node pointing at itself.

    After the swap the first node is at the end of the pair, so it becomes the predecessor for the next round.

    The loop condition checks that two nodes exist. When only one is left it stops, and that node stays where it is, which is what the problem asks for. And I use a dummy node in front because the head becomes the second node, so returning the original head would be wrong.

    This is the k-group reversal with k equals two, but writing it directly is clearer at this size. O(n) time, O(1) space. There's also a four-line recursive version, which is prettier but O(n) stack."

    Aur linked list reversal problems — practice list¶

    1. Reverse Linked List (LeetCode 206) — Problem 6.1. Yeh perfectly aana chahiye, muscle memory tak.
    2. Reverse Linked List II (92) — Problem 6.2.
    3. Reverse Nodes in k-Group (25) — Problem 6.3. Hard tag, bahut poocha jaata hai.
    4. Reverse alternating k-element sub-lists — Problem 6.4.
    5. Rotate List (61) — Problem 6.5.
    6. Swap Nodes in Pairs (24) — Problem 6.6.
    7. Palindrome Linked List (234) — Problem 3.5, reversal as sub-step.
    8. Reorder List (143) — Problem 3.7, reversal as sub-step.
    9. Add Two Numbers II (445) — digits forward order mein; reverse karo ya stacks use karo.
    10. Odd Even Linked List (328) — split aur reattach.
    11. Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups (2074) — variable group sizes.
    12. Remove Nth Node From End (19) — two pointers with gap.
    13. Merge Two Sorted Lists (21) — dummy node ka classic use.
    14. Merge k Sorted Lists (23) — Section 13.
    15. Sort List (148) — merge sort on linked list; middle plus merge.
    16. Copy List with Random Pointer (138) — interleave-and-split trick, same "rewire in place" skill.
    17. Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List (430) — recursion plus rewiring.
    18. Partition List (86) — do dummy nodes, do lists banao, jodo.
