    Toh agar hum har possible k ke liye "feasible hai ya nahi" likh dein:

    k:          1      2      3      4      5      6   ...  11
feasible:  No     No     No    YES    YES    YES  ...  YES
                              ^
                              |
                        yeh flip point hi answer hai

    Yeh exactly wahi shape hai jispar binary search chalta hai — ek sorted boolean array jismein Falses ke baad Trues hain. Hum us pehli True ki position dhoondh rahe hain.

    Toh: binary search on k (answer ki range), na ki piles par.

    Har mid ke liye ek feasibility check chalao (O(n)), aur uske hisaab se range aadhi karo.

    Yeh pattern "binary search on the answer" kehlata hai, aur uske teen zaroori hisse hain:

    1. Answer ki range [lo, hi] — kya sabse chhota aur sabse bada possible answer hai.
    2. Feasibility function is_feasible(x) — kya x kaam karta hai?
    3. Monotonicity — is_feasible ek hi direction mein flip karta hai. Bina iske binary search galat hoga.

    Optimal solution

    def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    def hours_needed(speed):                      # 1: FEASIBILITY helper
        total = 0                                 # 2
        for pile in piles:                        # 3: har pile
            total += (pile + speed - 1) // speed  # 4: integer CEILING division
        return total                              # 5

    low = 1                                       # 6: minimum possible speed
    high = max(piles)                             # 7: maximum USEFUL speed

    while low < high:                             # 8: Convention B -- `<`, `<=` nahi
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2             # 9: lower mid
        if hours_needed(mid) <= h:                # 10: `mid` speed par kaam ho jaata hai?
            high = mid                            # 11: mid CANDIDATE hai -- exclude mat karo
        else:                                     # 12: mid slow hai
            low = mid + 1                         # 13: isse tez chahiye

    return low                                    # 14: low == high == sabse chhoti feasible speed

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-5. Feasibility helper. Line 4: (pile + speed - 1) // speed — integer ceiling division. Kaise kaam karta hai: pile = 7, speed = 3 → (7 + 2) // 3 = 9 // 3 = 3. Sahi. pile = 6, speed = 3 → (6 + 2) // 3 = 8 // 3 = 2. Sahi (exact division par extra nahi jodta). math.ceil(pile / speed) bhi kaam karta hai lekin float division se guzarta hai, jo 10^18 type numbers par precision kho sakta hai. Integer version hamesha exact hai. 6. low = 1 — 0 nahi. Speed 0 par division by zero, aur logically bhi 0 speed se kuch nahi khaya jaata. 7. high = max(piles) — upper bound ka justification zaroori hai. Is speed par har pile exactly ek ghante mein khatam hoti hai (kyunki pile <= max(piles) = speed), toh total len(piles) ghante lagte hain. Problem guarantee deti hai h >= len(piles), toh yeh hamesha feasible hai. Isliye answer is range ke andar zaroor hai. Zyada bada high (jaise 10^9) bhi correct hoga — bas ek do extra iterations lagti. Lekin tight bound better hai. 8. while low < high: — Convention B. Yahan <= likhna infinite loop dega, kyunki line 11 mein high = mid hai (mid ko include karta hai). Agar low == high ho aur mid == low == high ho aur condition True ho, toh high = mid kuch nahi badalta. 9. mid = low + (high - low) // 2 — lower mid. Lower mid safe hai kyunki line 11 high = mid karti hai (range upar se shrink hoti hai) aur line 13 low = mid + 1 (range neeche se shrink hoti hai). Ek branch strictly shrink karti hai, toh progress guaranteed hai. Agar line 11 low = mid hoti toh upper mid chahiye hota — yeh section ke opener wala rule. 10. if hours_needed(mid) <= h: — <=, < nahi. h ghanton mein karna hai, toh exactly h ghante bhi valid hai. 11. high = mid — mid - 1 NAHI. Kyunki mid khud ek valid answer ho sakta hai — hum use discard nahi kar sakte. Hum sirf yeh jaante hain ki answer mid ya usse chhota hai. high = mid - 1 likhne se answer skip ho sakta hai. 12-13. mid slow hai → low = mid + 1. Yahan mid + 1 sahi hai kyunki mid definitely galat hai. 14. return low — loop ke baad low == high, aur woh sabse chhoti feasible speed hai. return high bhi bilkul same hai (dono barabar hain).

    Kyun return low sahi answer hai — invariant: loop ke dauraan hamesha yeh sach rehta hai ki "answer [low, high] range mein hai." Line 11 high ko us value par set karti hai jo feasible hai, aur line 13 low ko us value par jo infeasible se ek zyada hai. Jab range ek element par simat jaati hai, wahi answer hai.

    Dry run — piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8 (expected 4)

    low = 1, high = max = 11.

    Iter low high mid hours_needed(mid) <= 8? Action
    1 1 11 1 + 10//2 = 6 ceil(3/6)+ceil(6/6)+ceil(7/6)+ceil(11/6) = 1+1+2+2 = 6 Yes high = 6
    2 1 6 1 + 5//2 = 3 1+2+3+4 = 10 10 <= 8 No low = 4
    3 4 6 4 + 2//2 = 5 1+2+2+3 = 8 Yes high = 5
    4 4 5 4 + 1//2 = 4 1+2+2+3 = 8 Yes high = 4
    5 4 4 — — 4 < 4 False → exit —

    return low = 4. Sahi.

    Har row ka hours_needed detail: - mid = 6: ceil(3/6)=1, ceil(6/6)=1, ceil(7/6)=2, ceil(11/6)=2 → 6. - mid = 3: ceil(3/3)=1, ceil(6/3)=2, ceil(7/3)=3, ceil(11/3)=4 → 10. - mid = 5: ceil(3/5)=1, ceil(6/5)=2, ceil(7/5)=2, ceil(11/5)=3 → 8. - mid = 4: ceil(3/4)=1, ceil(6/4)=2, ceil(7/4)=2, ceil(11/4)=3 → 8.

    Iteration 4 sabse important hai — mid = 4 feasible tha aur high = mid = 4 kiya gaya, mid - 1 = 3 nahi. Agar high = mid - 1 likhte toh high = 3 hota aur low = 4 > high = 3 ke saath loop exit hota, phir return low = 4 — sanyog se sahi. Lekin dusre inputs par yeh skip kar deta. high = mid hi safe hai.

    Dry run — piles = [30, 11, 23, 4, 20], h = 5 (expected 30)

    low = 1, high = 30. Feasibility check ka pattern: h = 5 aur 5 piles hain, toh har pile exactly ek ghante mein khatam honi chahiye → speed >= max(piles) = 30.

    Iter low high mid hours <= 5? Action
    1 1 30 15 2+1+2+1+2 = 8 No low = 16
    2 16 30 23 2+1+1+1+1 = 6 No low = 24
    3 24 30 27 2+1+1+1+1 = 6 No low = 28
    4 28 30 29 2+1+1+1+1 = 6 No low = 30
    5 30 30 — — exit —

    return 30. Sahi.

    Dry run — same piles, h = 6 (expected 23)

    Iter low high mid hours <= 6? Action
    1 1 30 15 2+1+2+1+2 = 8 No low = 16
    2 16 30 23 2+1+1+1+1 = 6 Yes high = 23
    3 16 23 19 2+1+2+1+2 = 8 No low = 20
    4 20 23 21 2+1+2+1+1 = 7 No low = 22
    5 22 23 22 2+1+2+1+1 = 7 No low = 23
    6 23 23 — — exit —

    return 23. Sahi.

    Iteration 2 mein high = 23 set hua (mid ko include karke) — aur final answer exactly 23 hai. Agar high = mid - 1 = 22 likhte toh answer kabhi 23 nahi milta aur galat answer aata. Yeh line 11 ka poora justification hai.

    Complexity

    • Time: O(n log(max(piles))).
    • Binary search log(max(piles)) iterations chalata hai.
    • Har iteration mein feasibility check O(n) hai.
    • max(piles) = 10^9 par log = 30, toh 30n — linear se sirf 30 guna. Brute force O(n * max(piles)) tha — yeh 10^9 / 30 = 33 million guna faster hai.
    • Space: O(1).

    Edge cases

    Case piles h Output Kyun
    Single pile [10] 5 2 ceil(10/2) = 5
    h == len(piles) [3,6,7,11] 4 11 Har pile ek ghante mein
    h bahut bada [3,6,7,11] 100 1 Speed 1 kaafi hai
    All same [5,5,5] 3 5
    All ones [1,1,1] 3 1
    Very large pile [10**9] 1 10**9
    h < len(piles) [1,2] 1 Infeasible Problem guarantee deti hai h >= n

    Aakhri row important hai — agar h < len(piles) ho toh koi bhi speed kaam nahi karegi (har pile kam se kam ek ghanta leti hai). Problem yeh guarantee deti hai, lekin poochna chahiye. Bina guarantee ke code high = max(piles) return kar deta, jo galat hai — ek explicit check chahiye.

    Variations

    • Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (LeetCode 1011) — Problem 11.8.
    • Split Array Largest Sum (410) — same shape, "minimize the maximum subarray sum."
    • Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets (1482) — feasibility check thoda complex.
    • Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (1552) — "maximize the minimum" — monotonicity ulti direction mein hai, toh comparison flip karo.
    • Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station (774) — real-valued answer, toh while high - low > 1e-6 type loop.
    • Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold (1283) — bilkul Koko hi hai, alag kahani ke saath.
    • Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix (378) — binary search on value, counting feasibility check.

    Interview answer: "This one looks nothing like a binary search problem — the input isn't sorted and there's no target to find. But the answer space is what's searchable.

    Two observations set it up. First, the answer is bounded: the slowest useful speed is one, and the fastest useful speed is the largest pile, because at that speed every pile takes exactly one hour and eating faster can't help — you can't start a second pile in the same hour. Second, and this is the essential one, feasibility is monotonic: if speed k finishes in time, every faster speed does too. So if I laid out feasibility for every candidate speed I'd get a run of falses followed by a run of trues, and I'm looking for the first true.

    That's the shape binary search needs. So I binary search over speeds, and at each candidate I run an O(n) feasibility check summing the hours needed.

    Three implementation points.

    The hours calculation needs ceiling division, because a partial pile still consumes a whole hour. I write it as pile plus speed minus one, integer-divided by speed, rather than using math.ceil on a float division — with values up to a billion, float division can lose precision, while the integer form is always exact.

    When a candidate is feasible I set high equal to mid, not mid minus one, because that candidate might be the answer — I only know the answer is at or below it. That forces the loop condition to be a strict less-than; with less-than-or-equal it would hang, since setting high to mid when low equals high changes nothing.

    And because one branch keeps mid, I have to use the lower midpoint. If instead the code kept mid on the low side I'd need the upper midpoint. That's the general rule for avoiding infinite loops in this family.

    O(n log max-pile) time, O(1) space. With piles up to a billion that's about thirty passes over the array instead of a billion.

    I'd also confirm that h is at least the number of piles — otherwise no speed works at all, and the code would silently return the maximum pile rather than signalling infeasible."

    Problem 11.8 — Binary Search On The Answer: Split Array Largest Sum¶

    Problem statement

    Ek array nums (non-negative integers) aur ek number k diya hai. Array ko k contiguous subarrays mein baanto taaki sabse bade subarray ka sum minimum ho. Woh minimum value lauta do.

    Input:  nums = [7, 2, 5, 10, 8], k = 2
Output: 18
        Best split: [7, 2, 5] aur [10, 8]
        Sums: 14 aur 18. Maximum = 18.
        Koi aur split? [7,2,5,10] | [8] -> 24, 8 -> max 24. Bura.
                       [7,2] | [5,10,8] -> 9, 23 -> max 23. Bura.
        Toh 18 hi best hai.

Input:  nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2
Output: 9      ([1,2,3] | [4,5] -> 6, 9)

Input:  nums = [1, 4, 4], k = 3
Output: 4      (har element apna subarray)

    Yeh "minimize the maximum" phrase wali classic problem hai — aur woh phrase almost hamesha binary search on the answer ka signal hai.

    Ek bilkul same problem alag kahani ke saath: "Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days" (LeetCode 1011) — packages ko D din mein bhejna hai, ship ki minimum capacity kya ho. Wahi algorithm, alag naam.

    Pehla instinct — brute force (recursion)

    Har possible split try karo.

    def split_array_brute(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)                                 # 1

    def solve(start, parts):                      # 2: `start` se aage `parts` hisse banane hain
        if parts == 1:                            # 3: aakhri hissa -- sab bacha hua lo
            return sum(nums[start:])              # 4
        best = float('inf')                       # 5: minimum of maximums
        current_sum = 0                           # 6: pehle hisse ka sum
        # pehla hissa `start` se `i` tak (inclusive), baaki ke liye recursion
        for i in range(start, n - parts + 1):     # 7: BOUNDS -- neeche explanation
            current_sum += nums[i]                # 8: hissa badhao
            rest = solve(i + 1, parts - 1)        # 9: baaki ko recursively baanto
            best = min(best, max(current_sum, rest))   # 10: max lo, phir min track karo
        return best                               # 11

    return solve(0, k)                            # 12

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. Setup. 3-4. Base case: ek hissa bacha hai → sab bacha hua ek saath. 5. best = float('inf') — minimum track karna hai. 6-7. for i in range(start, n - parts + 1) — bounds ka logic: pehla hissa index start se i tak jaata hai. Baaki parts - 1 hisson ke liye kam se kam parts - 1 elements chahiye. Toh i at most n - (parts - 1) - 1 = n - parts tak ja sakta hai. range ka stop exclusive hai toh n - parts + 1. Yeh bound galat likhne se ya toh empty subarrays bante hain ya valid splits miss ho jaate. 8. current_sum += nums[i] — incremental sum (dobara compute nahi). 9. Recursion. 10. best = min(best, max(current_sum, rest)) — max phir min. max(current_sum, rest) — is split ka "largest sum". min(best, ...) — saare splits mein se sabse chhota largest sum. Yeh do-level nesting hi "minimize the maximum" ka literal translation hai. 11-12.

    Complexity: Time exponential — har position par split ya na split, roughly O(n^k) ya O(C(n, k)). n = 1000, k = 50 par impossible. Space O(k) recursion.

    Memoisation se DP: solve(start, parts) ko memoise karke O(n^2 * k) ho jaata hai — jo n = 1000, k = 50 par 5 * 10^7 hai, workable lekin slow.

    Isme problem kya hai

    Exponential (ya DP se bhi O(n^2 k)). Aur DP O(nk) space bhi leta hai. Binary search version O(n log(sum)) time aur O(1) space deta hai — bahut better.

    The insight

    Direct question mushkil hai: "best split kaunsa hai?"

    Ulta poocho: "kya ek split exist karta hai jismein har hisse ka sum at most X ho?"

    Yeh sawaal aasan hai — greedy se ek pass mein answer mil jaata hai: left se right chalo, ek hisse mein jitna daal sakte ho (limit X tak) daalte jao, aur limit cross hone par naya hissa shuru karo. Ant mein hisson ki count <= k hai toh answer haan.

    Aur yeh sawaal monotonic hai: - Agar X kaam karta hai (yaani X limit se <= k hisse bante hain), toh har bada X bhi kaam karega (aur bhi kam hisse banenge). - Agar X kaam nahi karta, toh har chhota X bhi nahi karega.

    X:          10     14     17     18     19    ...
feasible:   No     No     No    YES    YES    ...
                                ^
                          answer yahi hai

    Toh binary search on X (possible answers ki range), aur har X ke liye greedy feasibility check.

    Answer ki range: - low = max(nums) — kyunki sabse bada element apne aap ek hisse mein hoga, toh koi bhi hissa usse chhota nahi ho sakta. - high = sum(nums) — k = 1 par poora array ek hissa hai.

    Optimal solution

    def split_array(nums, k):
    def parts_needed(limit):                      # 1: FEASIBILITY -- greedy
        parts = 1                                 # 2: pehla hissa already shuru
        current = 0                               # 3: current hisse ka sum
        for num in nums:                          # 4: left se right
            if current + num > limit:             # 5: yeh element fit nahi hota
                parts += 1                        # 6: NAYA hissa shuru karo
                current = num                     # 7: naye hisse mein yeh element
            else:                                 # 8: fit ho jaata hai
                current += num                    # 9: current hisse mein daalo
        return parts                              # 10: kitne hisse lage

    low = max(nums)                               # 11: koi hissa isse chhota nahi ho sakta
    high = sum(nums)                              # 12: k=1 par poora array ek hissa

    while low < high:                             # 13: Convention B
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2             # 14: lower mid
        if parts_needed(mid) <= k:                # 15: `mid` limit se `k` ya kam hisse?
            high = mid                            # 16: mid CANDIDATE hai
        else:                                     # 17: `mid` limit se zyada hisse lagte hain
            low = mid + 1                         # 18: bada limit chahiye

    return low                                    # 19

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-10. Feasibility function — greedy, aur yeh greedy optimal kyun hai woh samajhna zaroori hai. Line 2: parts = 1 — 0 nahi. Hum pehle hisse ko already shuru maan lete hain; loop sirf naye hisse count karta hai. Line 5: if current + num > limit: — element fit nahi hota. Line 6-7: naya hissa shuru, aur current = num (na ki current = 0) — kyunki yeh element naye hisse mein jaa raha hai. Greedy kyun optimal hai: hum har hisse mein "jitna ho sake utna" bhar rahe hain. Agar hum kisi hisse ko jaldi band kar dein toh baad ke elements ke liye kam jagah bachti hai, toh zyada hisse lagenge. Toh greedy hamesha minimum hisse deta hai. Aur minimum hisse hi hum chahte hain (<= k check ke liye). Ek assumption: limit >= max(nums) — warna koi single element bhi fit nahi hoga aur parts galat aayega (infinite hisse chahiye). Line 11 yeh guarantee karti hai. 11. low = max(nums) — lower bound ka justification. Har element kisi na kisi hisse mein hoga, toh sabse bada element ka hissa kam se kam max(nums) hoga. Isse chhota answer possible hi nahi. low = 0 likhna galat nahi hoga (binary search phir bhi sahi answer dhoondh legi) lekin feasibility function crash kar sakta hai — limit = 0 par current + num > 0 hamesha True hoga aur parts n ho jaayega, jo technically theek hai. Lekin max(nums) tight bound hai aur iterations bachaata hai. 12. high = sum(nums) — upper bound. Poora array ek hissa. 13. while low < high: — Convention B (kyunki line 16 high = mid hai). 14. Lower mid. 15. if parts_needed(mid) <= k: — <=, == nahi. Agar mid limit se sirf 2 hisse lagte hain aur k = 3 hai, toh yeh feasible hai — hum 3 hisse bhi bana sakte hain (kisi hisse ko do mein tod kar), aur maximum sum sirf kam hi hoga. == k likhna galat hoga — bahut se valid mid reject ho jaate. 16. high = mid — mid candidate hai. 17-18. Infeasible → bada limit. 19. return low.

    Dry run — nums = [7, 2, 5, 10, 8], k = 2 (expected 18)

    low = max = 10, high = sum = 32.

    Iter low high mid parts_needed(mid) <= 2? Action
    1 10 32 10 + 22//2 = 21 see below → 2 Yes high = 21
    2 10 21 10 + 11//2 = 15 3 No low = 16
    3 16 21 16 + 5//2 = 18 2 Yes high = 18
    4 16 18 16 + 2//2 = 17 3 No low = 18
    5 18 18 — — 18 < 18 False → exit —

    return 18. Sahi.

    parts_needed ke traces:

    limit = 21: parts=1, current=0 - 7: 0+7 = 7 <= 21 → current = 7 - 2: 7+2 = 9 <= 21 → current = 9 - 5: 9+5 = 14 <= 21 → current = 14 - 10: 14+10 = 24 > 21 → parts = 2, current = 10 - 8: 10+8 = 18 <= 21 → current = 18 → parts = 2.

    limit = 15: parts=1, current=0 - 7: 7 <= 15 → current = 7 - 2: 9 <= 15 → current = 9 - 5: 14 <= 15 → current = 14 - 10: 24 > 15 → parts = 2, current = 10 - 8: 18 > 15 → parts = 3, current = 8 → parts = 3. 3 <= 2 False.

    limit = 18: parts=1, current=0 - 7, 2, 5 → current = 14 - 10: 24 > 18 → parts = 2, current = 10 - 8: 18 <= 18 → current = 18 (exactly at the limit) → parts = 2. Feasible.

    limit = 17: 7,2,5 → 14. 10: 24 > 17 → parts=2, current=10. 8: 18 > 17 → parts=3. Infeasible.

    limit = 18 aur limit = 17 ka contrast hi answer 18 banata hai — 18 par [7,2,5] aur [10,8] bilkul fit ho jaate hain (sums 14 aur 18), 17 par nahi.

    Iteration 3 par high = mid = 18 set hua, mid - 1 = 17 nahi. Agar high = mid - 1 likhte toh high = 17 hota aur answer 18 kabhi nahi milta. Yeh line 16 ka poora justification hai — aur is problem mein woh visible hai (Koko mein sanyog se dono kaam kar gaye the).

    Dry run — nums = [1, 4, 4], k = 3 (expected 4)

    low = 4, high = 9.

    Iter low high mid parts_needed(mid) <= 3? Action
    1 4 9 6 1+4=5 <= 6 → current=5; 5+4=9 > 6 → parts=2, current=4 → 2 Yes high = 6
    2 4 6 5 1+4=5 <= 5 → current=5; 5+4=9 > 5 → parts=2 → 2 Yes high = 5
    3 4 5 4 1+4=5 > 4 → parts=2, current=4; 4+4=8 > 4 → parts=3 → 3 3 <= 3 Yes high = 4
    4 4 4 — — exit —

    return 4. Sahi — har element apna hissa.

    Iteration 3 line 15 ke <= ko justify karta hai — parts_needed(4) = 3 exactly k ke barabar hai, aur woh feasible hai.

    Complexity

    • Time: O(n * log(sum(nums) - max(nums))).
    • Binary search range ka size sum - max hai, toh log(sum) iterations.
    • Har iteration O(n) feasibility check.
    • n = 1000 aur values 10^6 tak → sum = 10^9 → log = 30 → 30,000 operations. Bahut fast. DP version O(n^2 * k) tha — n=1000, k=50 par 5 * 10^7. Binary search 1000 guna faster hai.
    • Space: O(1). DP version O(nk) leta hai.

    Edge cases

    Case nums k Output Kyun
    k = 1 [1,2,3] 1 6 Poora array ek hissa; low high tak chadhta
    k = n [1,2,3] 3 3 Har element apna; answer max(nums)
    k > n [1,2] 5 2 Extra hisse khaali; answer max(nums)
    Single element [5] 1 5 low = high = 5
    All same [4,4,4] 2 8 [4,4] aur [4]
    Zeros [0,0,0] 2 0 low = 0, high = 0
    One huge element [1,1,100] 2 100 low = 100 se hi shuru
    Empty [] 1 Crash max([]) ValueError — guard chahiye

    "Zeros" wala case interesting hai — low = max = 0 aur high = sum = 0, toh loop chalta hi nahi aur return 0. Sahi.

    "Empty" wala case guard maangta hai — max([]) aur sum([]) mein se pehla crash karta hai. Problem usually n >= 1 guarantee deti hai, lekin poochna chahiye.

    Variations

    • Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (LeetCode 1011) — bilkul yehi problem. weights aur days, answer minimum ship capacity.
    • Koko Eating Bananas (875) — Problem 11.7, same shape.
    • Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets (1482) — feasibility check thoda complex (consecutive flowers).
    • Divide Chocolate (1231) — "maximize the minimum" — ulti monotonicity, comparison flip karo.
    • Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (1552) — maximize the minimum distance.
    • Minimum Limit of Balls in a Bag (1760) — same shape, alag feasibility.
    • Maximum Number of Removable Characters (1898) — binary search on count.

    Ek general recipe jo saare "binary search on the answer" problems par lagti hai:

    1. Poocho: "kya ek candidate answer X ke liye feasibility check O(n) mein ho sakta hai?"
    2. Poocho: "kya feasibility monotonic hai?" (X kaam karta hai → X+1 bhi karta hai, ya ulta)
    3. Answer ki range ke tight bounds nikaalo.
    4. Binary search, aur jo boundary candidate ho sakti hai use mid par set karo, mid ± 1 par nahi.

    Interview answer: "The direct question — which split is best — leads to an exponential search, or O(n squared times k) with dynamic programming. So I invert it.

    Instead of 'what's the best split', I ask 'is there a split where every part sums to at most X?' That question is easy: walk left to right greedily, packing as much as fits into the current part and starting a new one when it doesn't. Greedy gives the minimum number of parts for that limit, because closing a part early only leaves less room later. Then X works if that minimum is at most k.

    And that predicate is monotonic — a larger limit never needs more parts. So feasibility over the candidate answers is a run of falses followed by a run of trues, and I binary search for the first true.

    The bounds matter. The low end is the maximum element, because whichever part contains it can't sum to less than that — and that bound also keeps the greedy check well-defined, since with a smaller limit no single element would fit. The high end is the total sum, which is the k-equals-one case.

    Two details in the search itself. The feasibility test is 'parts needed is at most k', not 'exactly k' — if a limit only needs two parts and k is three, that's still feasible, since I can always split a part further and only lower the maximum. And when a candidate is feasible I set high to mid, not mid minus one, because that candidate might be the answer. In this problem that's visibly load-bearing: the answer eighteen is found exactly at a mid, and moving past it would lose it.

    That gives O(n log sum) time and O(1) space, versus O(n squared k) time and O(nk) space for the DP.

    The general recipe I'd state: if I can check a candidate answer in linear time and feasibility is monotonic in that answer, I can binary search the answer space regardless of whether the input is sorted. The phrases 'minimize the maximum' and 'maximize the minimum' are almost always this pattern."

    Aur modified binary search problems — practice list¶

    Classic binary search variants:

    1. Binary Search (LeetCode 704) — base.
    2. Order-agnostic binary search — Problem 11.1.
    3. Search Insert Position (35) — ceiling ka index.
    4. Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target (744) — Problem 11.3.
    5. Find First and Last Position of Element (34) — Problem 11.4. Zaroor karo.
    6. Ceiling/floor of a number — Problem 11.2.
    7. Find K Closest Elements (658) — binary search plus two pointers.
    8. Peak Index in a Mountain Array (852) — bitonic peak.
    9. Find Peak Element (162) — unsorted array par binary search. Interesting kyunki input sorted nahi hai.
    10. Search a 2D Matrix (74) — flatten karke normal binary search.
    11. Search a 2D Matrix II (240) — staircase search, O(m+n).

    Rotated arrays:

    1. Search in Rotated Sorted Array (33) — Problem 11.5. Zaroor karo.
    2. Search in Rotated Sorted Array II (81) — duplicates, O(n) worst case.
    3. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (153) — pivot dhoondo.
    4. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II (154) — duplicates ke saath.

    Infinite / unknown bounds:

    1. Search in a Sorted Array of Unknown Size (702) — Problem 11.6.
    2. First Bad Version (278) — binary search on the answer ka sabse simple example. API calls minimise karni hain.
    3. Guess Number Higher or Lower (374) — interactive binary search.

    Binary search on the answer (yeh sabse valuable group hai):

    1. Koko Eating Bananas (875) — Problem 11.7. Zaroor karo.
    2. Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (1011) — Problem 11.8 ka twin.
    3. Split Array Largest Sum (410) — Problem 11.8. Hard tag.

    Ek line mein poore pattern ka summary:

    Do bilkul alag families hain. Pehli — input sorted hai aur aap ek position dhoondh rahe ho; yahan sirf boundary conventions aur "match par turant return karne ki jagah save karke aage dhoondhna" seekhna hai. Dusri — input sorted nahi hai lekin answer space par monotonicity hai; yahan aap answers ki range par search karte ho aur har candidate ko ek O(n) feasibility check se test karte ho. Dusri family zyada valuable hai kyunki woh kam obvious hai aur zyada problems cover karti hai.

    Aur ek chhoti si checklist jo har binary search likhne se pehle mentally chala lo:

    Sawaal Kyun
    high len(arr) hai ya len(arr) - 1? Loop condition isse judi hai
    Loop < hai ya <=? high ke choice se match honi chahiye
    Koi branch mid ko include karti hai? Toh mid ka calculation (lower/upper) adjust karo
    Har branch range shrink karti hai? Warna infinite loop
    Match par return karna hai ya save karke aage dhoondhna? Exact search vs boundary search
    Feasibility genuinely monotonic hai? Warna binary search on answer galat hai

    12. Top K Elements¶

    Recognition signals — aap top K dekh rahe ho jab problem bole¶

    • "top K", "K largest", "K smallest", "Kth largest", "Kth smallest".
    • "K most frequent", "K closest", "K best" — kisi bhi metric par.
    • "find the K ... " jahan K poore input se bahut chhota ho.
    • Problem sorting suggest kare lekin poora sorted order chahiye na ho — sirf top K chahiye.
    • Streaming data ho aur har point par top K chahiye ho.
    • Constraint bole O(n log k) ya O(k) space — yeh heap ka signature hai.

    Yeh pattern kaam kyun karta hai — asli intuition¶

    Sabse obvious solution hai: poora sort karo, phir pehle K le lo. Woh O(n log n) hai.

    Lekin socho — agar n = 10^6 aur k = 10 hai, toh hum ek million elements ko poori tarah order kar rahe hain jabki humein sirf 10 chahiye. 999,990 elements ka relative order bilkul irrelevant hai.

    Heap yeh waste hataata hai: size k ka heap rakho. Har naya element aaye toh dekho ki woh current top-K mein aata hai ya nahi. Agar haan toh sabse "kamzor" element bahar phenk do.

    Do fayde: 1. Time O(n log k) — log k log n se bahut chhota hai jab k << n. 2. Space O(k) — poora array memory mein rakhne ki zaroorat nahi. Streaming data ke liye yeh critical hai.

    Sabse important rule — heap ki direction ulti hoti hai¶

    Yeh sabse zyada confuse karne wali baat hai, aur interview mein sabse zyada galat hoti hai:

    Chahiye Heap type Kyun
    K LARGEST elements MIN-heap of size k Top par sabse kamzor candidate hota hai — use hi bahar phenkna hai
    K SMALLEST elements MAX-heap of size k Top par sabse kamzor candidate (sabse bada) hota hai

    Ulta kyun? Kyunki heap ka top hi ekmatra element hai jise hum O(1) mein dekh aur O(log k) mein hata sakte hain. Aur hum hamesha sabse kharab element hataana chahte hain.

    Agar K largest chahiye, toh sabse kharab candidate sabse chhota hai — toh use top par hona chahiye — toh min-heap.

    Ek line mein yaad rakhne ka tarika: heap ka top woh element hona chahiye jise aap sabse pehle nikaalna chahenge.

    Python mein max-heap¶

    heapq sirf min-heap deta hai. Max-heap ke liye values negate karo:

    import heapq

max_heap = []
heapq.heappush(max_heap, -value)      # push par negate
largest = -max_heap[0]                # peek par wapas negate
largest = -heapq.heappop(max_heap)    # pop par wapas negate

    Tuples ke saath: agar (key, value) push kar rahe ho aur max-heap chahiye, toh sirf key negate karo: (-key, value).

    Aur ek gotcha: agar keys tie karein toh Python value compare karega. Agar value comparable nahi hai (jaise ek custom object) toh TypeError aata hai. Fix: ek unique integer tie-breaker daalo: (-key, counter, value).

    Teen alag approaches — aur unke trade-offs¶

    Approach Time Space Kab use karo
    Sort O(n log n) O(n) k n ke barabar ho; ya code simplicity chahiye
    Heap of size k O(n log k) O(k) k << n; streaming data; memory constrained
    Quickselect O(n) average O(1) kth element chahiye, order nahi; static array; worst case O(n^2)

    Interview mein teenon mention karo aur trade-off bolo — yeh sabse strong signal hai ki aapne sirf ek solution ratta nahi maara.

    Template code¶

    import heapq

def k_largest(nums, k):
    """K sabse bade elements. MIN-heap of size k."""
    heap = []                              # min-heap
    for num in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, num)          # daal do
        if len(heap) > k:                  # size k se bada?
            heapq.heappop(heap)            # sabse CHHOTA nikaal do (woh top-k mein nahi)
    return heap                            # heap mein k sabse bade hain (unsorted)


def k_smallest(nums, k):
    """K sabse chhote elements. MAX-heap of size k (negation se)."""
    heap = []                              # max-heap via negation
    for num in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, -num)         # negate karke push
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)            # sabse BADA nikaal do
    return [-x for x in heap]              # wapas negate karke lauta do

    Template ka core idea: har element ko heap mein daalo, aur size k se upar jaate hi sabse kharab wala hata do. Heap ka size kabhi k se upar nahi jaata, toh har operation O(log k) hai.

    Ek optimisation jo mention karne layak hai: heappush phir heappop ki jagah, jab heap already bhara ho toh heapq.heappushpop(heap, num) use karo — woh dono ko ek hi sift operation mein karta hai.

    Problem 12.1 — Top K Numbers¶

    Problem statement

    Unsorted array aur ek number k diya hai. K sabse bade elements lauta do. Order matter nahi karta.

    Input:  nums = [3, 1, 5, 12, 2, 11], k = 3
Output: [5, 12, 11]     (koi bhi order)

Input:  nums = [5, 12, 11, -1, 12], k = 3
Output: [12, 11, 12]

    Pehla instinct — brute force

    Sort karo, phir aakhri k le lo.

    def top_k_sort(nums, k):
    nums_sorted = sorted(nums)                    # 1: ascending, O(n log n)
    return nums_sorted[-k:]                       # 2: aakhri k elements

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1. sorted(nums) — sorted use kiya, .sort() nahi, taaki caller ka array na badle.
    2. nums_sorted[-k:] — negative slicing aakhri k elements deta hai. Edge case: agar k > len(nums) ho toh yeh poora array deta hai (crash nahi karta) — jo reasonable behaviour hai. Edge case: agar k == 0 ho toh nums_sorted[0:] — poora array! Yeh ek silent bug hai. nums_sorted[-0:] mein -0 == 0 hai, toh slice [0:] ban jaata hai. Guard chahiye: if k == 0: return [].

    Complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n) (copy).

    Ya Python ka built-in:

    import heapq

def top_k_builtin(nums, k):
    return heapq.nlargest(k, nums)                # 3: ek line

    Line 3: heapq.nlargest internally exactly wahi heap technique use karta hai — O(n log k). Production mein yehi likhna chahiye. Interview mein mention karo lekin manual version bhi likho, kyunki test wahi ho raha hai.

    Isme problem kya hai

    Sort wala version: 1. O(n log n) jab O(n log k) possible hai. 2. O(n) space — poora array memory mein. Streaming data par yeh possible hi nahi hai. 3. Hum n - k elements ka relative order compute kar rahe hain jiski koi zaroorat nahi.

    The insight

    Ek min-heap of size k rakho.

    Kyun min-heap jab hum largest chahte hain? Kyunki heap ka top hi accessible hai, aur hum hamesha sabse chhota candidate hataana chahte hain (kyunki woh top-K mein sabse kamzor hai). Min-heap ka top = sabse chhota. Perfect.

    Process: har element push karo. Agar heap size k se upar chala gaya, toh top (sabse chhota) pop kar do. Ant mein heap mein exactly k sabse bade elements bache honge.

    Optimal solution

    import heapq

def top_k_numbers(nums, k):
    if k <= 0:                                    # 1: guard -- k=0 ya negative
        return []                                 # 2
    heap = []                                     # 3: MIN-heap, size at most k

    for num in nums:                              # 4: har element ek baar
        if len(heap) < k:                         # 5: heap abhi bhara nahi
            heapq.heappush(heap, num)             # 6: bas daal do
        elif num > heap[0]:                       # 7: naya element top-k mein aata hai?
            heapq.heappushpop(heap, num)          # 8: push + pop ek saath

    return heap                                   # 9: k sabse bade (unsorted order mein)

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. k <= 0 guard. Bina iske k = 0 par heap khaali rehta (line 5 0 < 0 False, line 7 heap[0] par IndexError). Guard zaroori hai. 3. heap = [] — min-heap. Koi negation nahi, kyunki hum largest chahte hain. 4. for num in nums: — ek hi pass. 5-6. if len(heap) < k: — heap abhi k elements se kam rakhta hai → bina soche push karo. Yeh branch pehle k elements ke liye chalti hai. 7. elif num > heap[0]: — heap[0] = current top-k ka sabse chhota element. Agar naya element usse bada hai toh woh top-k mein aata hai (aur heap[0] bahar jaata hai). Agar chhota ya barabar hai toh kuch mat karo — woh top-k mein nahi aata. > hai, >= nahi — barabar hone par swap karne ka koi fayda nahi (result same rahega), bas ek faltu O(log k) operation. 8. heapq.heappushpop(heap, num) — push aur pop ek saath. heappush phir heappop likhne se do sift operations hoti hain; heappushpop ek karta hai. Same complexity O(log k), better constant factor. Aur yeh safe hai kyunki line 7 ne guarantee kiya ki num > heap[0] — toh heappushpop heap[0] ko hi pop karega, naye element ko nahi. 9. return heap — unsorted order mein. Heap ka internal order sorted nahi hota — sirf heap property (parent <= children) satisfy hoti hai. Agar sorted output chahiye toh sorted(heap, reverse=True) — extra O(k log k). Problem "koi bhi order" kehti hai, toh yeh theek hai. Clarify karo.

    Ek simpler (thoda slower) version jo bhi bilkul correct hai:

    def top_k_simple(nums, k):
    heap = []                                     # 10
    for num in nums:                              # 11
        heapq.heappush(heap, num)                 # 12: hamesha push
        if len(heap) > k:                         # 13: size k se upar?
            heapq.heappop(heap)                   # 14: sabse chhota nikaal do
    return heap                                   # 15

    Yeh har element ko push karta hai (chahe woh top-k mein na aata ho) aur phir pop karta hai. Optimal version un elements ko skip kar deta hai jo heap[0] se chhote hain — jo practically zyadatar elements hote hain. Same asymptotic O(n log k), lekin constant factor kaafi behtar.

    Dry run — nums = [3, 1, 5, 12, 2, 11], k = 3 (expected top-3 = {5, 11, 12})

    Step num len(heap) < 3? heap[0] num > heap[0]? Action heap (top first)
    init — — — — — []
    1 3 0 < 3 Yes — — push [3]
    2 1 1 < 3 Yes — — push [1, 3]
    3 5 2 < 3 Yes — — push [1, 3, 5]
    4 12 3 < 3 No 1 12 > 1 Yes pushpop [3, 12, 5]
    5 2 No 3 2 > 3 No skip [3, 12, 5]
    6 11 No 3 11 > 3 Yes pushpop [5, 12, 11]

    Result [5, 12, 11] — top-3 hain {5, 11, 12}. Sahi.

    Step 5 sabse important hai — 2 ke liye koi heap operation nahi hui, sirf ek comparison. Yeh optimal version ka poora fayda hai — simple version yahan ek push aur ek pop karta.

    Step 4 ko dekho — heap[0] 1 tha (sabse chhota), aur 12 usse bada tha, toh 1 bahar aur 12 andar. Heap ka naya top 3 ban gaya.

    Dry run — duplicates — nums = [5, 12, 11, -1, 12], k = 3

    Step num heap before Action heap after
    1 5 [] push [5]
    2 12 [5] push [5, 12]
    3 11 [5, 12] push [5, 12, 11]
    4 -1 [5, 12, 11] -1 > 5? No → skip [5, 12, 11]
    5 12 [5, 12, 11] 12 > 5? Yes → pushpop [11, 12, 12]

    Result [11, 12, 12] — duplicates dono rakhe gaye. Sahi (top-3 by value, distinct nahi).

    Complexity

    • Time: O(n log k).
    • n elements, har ek par at most ek O(log k) heap operation.
    • Practically kam — jo elements heap[0] se chhote hain unpar sirf O(1) comparison hoti hai.
    • Compare with sorting: n = 10^6, k = 10 par log k = 3.3 vs log n = 20 — 6 guna faster.
    • Space: O(k). Heap mein at most k elements. Poora array kabhi memory mein nahi aata — streaming ke liye critical.

    Edge cases

    Case nums k Output Kyun
    k = 0 [1,2,3] 0 [] Line 1 guard
    k > n [1,2] 5 [1,2] Heap kabhi bharta nahi
    k == n [1,2,3] 3 [1,2,3] Poora array
    Empty [] 3 [] Loop chalta nahi
    All same [5,5,5] 2 [5,5] Duplicates allowed
    Negatives [-5,-1,-3] 2 [-3,-1] Comparison natural
    Single [5] 1 [5]
    k negative [1,2] -1 [] Guard

    Variations

    • Kth largest element (LeetCode 215) — Problem 12.2; heap[0] hi answer hai.
    • K smallest — max-heap (negation) ya heapq.nsmallest.
    • Top K sorted order mein — sorted(heap, reverse=True), extra O(k log k).
    • Top K frequent (347) — Problem 12.5; pehle frequency count karo.
    • Streaming top K — yehi code, class ke roop mein (Problem 9.5 jaisa).
    • Top K by a custom key — heap mein (key(x), x) tuples daalo.
    • Quickselect — O(n) average, lekin poora array chahiye aur streaming par kaam nahi karta.

    Interview answer: "Sorting and taking the last k works and is O(n log n), but it computes the full ordering of all n elements when I only care about k of them. With a million elements and k of ten, that's a lot of wasted comparisons — and it needs the whole array in memory, so it doesn't work on a stream at all.

    Instead I keep a heap of size k. The direction is the part that trips people up: for the k largest elements I use a min-heap. The reason is that the top of a heap is the only element I can cheaply inspect and remove, and the one I always want to remove is the weakest candidate — which, when collecting the largest, is the smallest one. So the smallest has to be at the top, which means a min-heap.

    Then it's one pass. While the heap has fewer than k elements, just push. Once it's full, compare the incoming value against the heap's top: if it's larger, it belongs in the top k and displaces the top; if it isn't, I skip it entirely with a single comparison and no heap operation at all. In practice that skip covers most elements.

    When it does displace, I use heappushpop rather than a push followed by a pop, which does it in one sift instead of two.

    O(n log k) time and O(k) space. The space bound is the real win — it's what makes this work on a stream.

    I'd also mention the third option: quickselect gets the kth element in O(n) average time, which beats the heap, but it needs random access to the whole array, mutates it, and has an O(n squared) worst case. So heap for streams and bounded memory, quickselect for a static array where I just need the kth value.

    Two small things I'd confirm: whether the output needs to be sorted — the heap's contents aren't in order — and I'd guard k of zero explicitly, because negative slicing on the sorted version silently returns the entire array."

    Problem 12.2 — Kth Smallest Number¶

    Problem statement

    Unsorted array aur ek number k diya hai. Kth smallest element lauta do (1-indexed — k = 1 matlab sabse chhota).

    Input:  nums = [1, 5, 12, 2, 11, 5], k = 3
Output: 5      (sorted: [1, 2, 5, 5, 11, 12], teesra = 5)

Input:  nums = [5, 12, 11, -1, 12], k = 3
Output: 11     (sorted: [-1, 5, 11, 12, 12], teesra = 11)

Input:  nums = [3, 2, 1], k = 1
Output: 1

    Dhyaan do: duplicates alag elements ginte hain. [1, 5, 5] mein 2nd smallest 5 hai, 5 nahi... balki hai — 2nd smallest 5 hi hai.

    Pehla instinct — brute force

    Sort karo aur index k-1 le lo.

    def kth_smallest_sort(nums, k):
    return sorted(nums)[k - 1]                    # 1: `k-1` kyunki 1-indexed -> 0-indexed

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1. sorted(nums)[k - 1] — k - 1 zaroori hai. k = 1 → index 0 → sabse chhota. k = 3 → index 2 → teesra. Sahi. k likhna ek off-by-one bug hai jo kth ki jagah (k+1)th deta. Agar k > len(nums) ho toh IndexError — guard chahiye.

    Complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n).

    Isme problem kya hai

    Wahi Problem 12.1 wali baat — poora sort jab sirf ek element chahiye.

    The insight — teen alag approaches

    Approach A — max-heap of size k. K smallest chahiye, toh max-heap rakho (Problem 12.1 ka ulta). Heap mein k sabse chhote elements rahenge, aur uska top hi kth smallest hoga.

    Kyun max-heap? Kyunki hum sabse bada candidate hataana chahte hain (woh k-smallest mein sabse kamzor hai). Max-heap ka top = sabse bada. Perfect.

    Approach B — min-heap, k pops. Poore array ka min-heap banao (heapify O(n)), phir k-1 baar pop karo. kth pop hi answer hai. - Time: O(n + k log n). - k chhota hone par yeh Approach A se better hai (O(n) dominate karta hai). k bada hone par bura.

    Approach C — quickselect. Quicksort ka partition step use karo, lekin sirf ek side mein recurse karo (kyunki k batata hai ki answer kaunsi side hai). - Time: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst case (bad pivots). - Space O(1) (in-place). - Sabse fast average case, lekin array mutate karta hai aur streaming par kaam nahi karta.

    Teenon ka trade-off bolna interview mein bahut strong hai.

    Optimal solution — Approach A (max-heap of size k)

    import heapq

def kth_smallest_heap(nums, k):
    if k <= 0 or k > len(nums):                   # 1: invalid k guard
        raise ValueError("k out of range")        # 2

    heap = []                                     # 3: MAX-heap via negation
    for num in nums:                              # 4
        if len(heap) < k:                         # 5: heap abhi bhara nahi
            heapq.heappush(heap, -num)            # 6: NEGATE karke push
        elif num < -heap[0]:                      # 7: naya element k-smallest mein aata hai?
            heapq.heappushpop(heap, -num)         # 8: negate, push, pop ek saath

    return -heap[0]                               # 9: top = sabse BADA of k smallest = kth smallest

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. Guard. k = 0 par line 9 heap[0] IndexError deta. k > n par heap kabhi k elements tak nahi bharta aur answer galat hota. raise kiya, return None nahi — kyunki invalid input silently galat answer se better hai ki explicitly fail ho. Interview mein clarify karo ki caller kya expect karta hai. 3. heap = [] — max-heap via negation. 4-6. Pehle k elements bina soche push (negate karke). 7. elif num < -heap[0]: — -heap[0] = heap ka actual maximum. Negation ki wajah se heap[0] sabse chhota negated value hai, jo sabse bada actual value hai. Agar naya num usse chhota hai toh woh k-smallest mein aata hai. -heap[0] likhna bhoolna sabse common bug hai — num < heap[0] likhne se comparison negated value se hoti hai, jo bilkul ulta result deta. 8. heapq.heappushpop(heap, -num) — -num push kiya. Yeh line mein do negations hain (-heap[0] line 7 mein aur -num yahan) aur dono zaroori hain. Yeh negation-based max-heap ki sabse badi lagat hai — mental overhead. 9. return -heap[0] — top ko un-negate karke lauta do. Heap mein k sabse chhote elements hain, aur uska top unme se sabse bada hai — jo exactly kth smallest hai.

    Optimal solution — Approach C (quickselect)

    import random

def kth_smallest_quickselect(nums, k):
    nums = list(nums)                             # 10: COPY -- caller ka array mutate na ho
    target_index = k - 1                          # 11: 1-indexed -> 0-indexed
    low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1                  # 12

    while low <= high:                            # 13
        pivot_index = partition(nums, low, high)  # 14: pivot ko uski FINAL jagah par bhejo
        if pivot_index == target_index:           # 15: exactly wahi position?
            return nums[pivot_index]              # 16: mil gaya
        elif pivot_index < target_index:          # 17: answer daaye mein
            low = pivot_index + 1                 # 18
        else:                                     # 19: answer baaye mein
            high = pivot_index - 1                # 20
    raise ValueError("k out of range")            # 21


def partition(nums, low, high):
    # RANDOM pivot -- sorted input par O(n^2) se bachne ke liye
    rand_index = random.randint(low, high)        # 22
    nums[rand_index], nums[high] = nums[high], nums[rand_index]   # 23: pivot ko end par le jao

    pivot = nums[high]                            # 24: pivot value
    store = low                                   # 25: chhote elements ki agli jagah

    for i in range(low, high):                    # 26: pivot ko chhod kar sab
        if nums[i] < pivot:                       # 27: pivot se chhota?
            nums[store], nums[i] = nums[i], nums[store]   # 28: aage bhej do
            store += 1                            # 29

    nums[store], nums[high] = nums[high], nums[store]      # 30: pivot ko uski jagah par
    return store                                  # 31: pivot ka FINAL index

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1. nums = list(nums) — copy. Quickselect array ko reorder karta hai; caller ka data corrupt karna surprising side effect hai.
    2. target_index = k - 1. 12-13. Binary-search-jaisa loop.
    3. partition(...) — pivot ko uski final sorted position par bhej deta hai, aur uske left mein sab chhote, right mein sab bade. 15-16. Agar pivot exactly target_index par hai toh wahi answer hai — chahe baaki array sorted na ho. 17-20. Ek hi side mein continue karo. Yehi quickselect ko quicksort se alag banata hai — quicksort dono sides mein recurse karta hai (O(n log n)), quickselect ek (O(n) average).
    4. Guard. 22-23. Random pivot — yeh line critical hai. Bina randomisation ke, agar array already sorted ho toh pivot hamesha sabse bada element hoga aur partition har baar sirf ek element alag karega → O(n^2). Random pivot se average case O(n) rehta hai. Yeh interview mein zaroor mention karna chahiye. 24-25. Lomuto partition scheme setup. 26-29. Chhote elements ko aage bhejo. store ek boundary hai: [low, store) mein sab < pivot hain. nums[i] < pivot par swap aur store badhao. < hai, <= nahi — duplicates ke saath <= bhi kaam karta hai lekin partition unbalanced ho jaata hai (saare duplicates ek side).
    5. Pivot ko store position par bhej do — wahi uski final sorted position hai.
    6. Return.

    Dry run — heap version — nums = [1, 5, 12, 2, 11, 5], k = 3 (expected 5)

    Heap mein negated values store hoti hain. Table mein maine actual values dikhaye hain (-heap[0] = max).

    Step num len(heap) < 3? heap (actual values) max = -heap[0] num < max? Action
    init — — {} — — —
    1 1 Yes {1} 1 — push
    2 5 Yes {1, 5} 5 — push
    3 12 Yes {1, 5, 12} 12 — push
    4 2 No — 12 2 < 12 Yes pushpop → {1, 5, 2}
    5 11 No {1, 5, 2} 5 11 < 5 No skip
    6 5 No {1, 5, 2} 5 5 < 5 No skip

    return -heap[0] = 5. Sahi.

    Step 4 ko dekho — 12 (sabse bada) bahar gaya aur 2 andar. Heap mein ab {1, 2, 5} hain — 3 sabse chhote. Top = 5 = 3rd smallest.

    Step 6 important hai — 5 aur heap ka max dono 5 hain. < strict hone ki wajah se skip hua. Kya yeh sahi hai? Haan — agar swap karte toh heap {1, 2, 5} hi rehta (ek 5 bahar, doosra 5 andar), answer same. Bas ek faltu operation bach gaya.

    Dry run — quickselect — nums = [1, 5, 12, 2, 11, 5], k = 3, target_index = 2

    Maan lo random pivot 5 (index 1) chuna gaya.

    Partition 1 (low=0, high=5): - rand_index = 1 → swap nums[1] aur nums[5] → [1, 5, 12, 2, 11, 5] (dono 5 hain, koi visible change nahi). - pivot = nums[5] = 5, store = 0.

    i nums[i] < 5? Action nums store
    0 1 Yes swap(0,0), store=1 [1,5,12,2,11,5] 1
    1 5 No — same 1
    2 12 No — same 1
    3 2 Yes swap(1,3), store=2 [1,2,12,5,11,5] 2
    4 11 No — same 2
    • Line 30: swap(2, 5) → [1, 2, 5, 5, 11, 12]. return 2.

    Line 15: pivot_index = 2 == target_index = 2 → return nums[2] = 5. Sahi, ek hi partition mein.

    Complexity

    Approach Time Space Notes
    Sort O(n log n) O(n) Simplest
    Max-heap size k O(n log k) O(k) Streaming-friendly
    Min-heap + k pops O(n + k log n) O(n) Chhote k par best
    Quickselect O(n) avg, O(n^2) worst O(1) Fastest avg, mutates input

    Kaunsa chunein — decision rule: - k chhota aur data streaming → heap. - Static array, sirf value chahiye, memory tight → quickselect. - k n ke barabar ya code simplicity chahiye → sort.

    Edge cases

    Case nums k Output Kyun
    k = 1 [3,1,2] 1 1 Minimum
    k = n [3,1,2] 3 3 Maximum
    k = 0 [1,2] 0 Error Guard
    k > n [1,2] 5 Error Guard
    All same [5,5,5] 2 5 Duplicates alag ginte hain
    Duplicates at k [1,5,5,12] 2 5
    Negatives [-5,-1,-3] 2 -3
    Single [7] 1 7
    Sorted input (quickselect) [1,2,...,10^6] 1 1 Random pivot ke bina O(n^2)

    Aakhri row quickselect ka randomisation justify karta hai.

    Variations

    • Kth largest (LeetCode 215) — min-heap of size k, ya quickselect with n - k index.
    • Kth largest in a stream (703) — Problem 9.5.
    • Kth smallest in a sorted matrix (378) — binary search on value, ya k-way merge heap. Section 13.
    • Kth smallest in a BST (230) — inorder traversal, kth element par ruk jao. O(h + k).
    • Median — k = n // 2 (ya do values ka average).
    • Kth smallest distinct — pehle dedupe karo.
    • Kth smallest pair sum / product — binary search on the answer plus counting.

    Interview answer: "Three reasonable approaches, and which one I'd pick depends on the constraints.

    Sorting and indexing is one line and O(n log n) — fine if k is close to n or if clarity matters most.

    A heap of size k gives O(n log k) time and, more importantly, O(k) space, so it works on a stream. The direction flips from the intuitive one: for the k smallest elements I keep a max-heap, because the element I want to evict is the largest of the ones I'm holding, and only the heap's top is cheap to remove. When the heap is full, an incoming value replaces the top only if it's smaller. At the end, the top of the heap is the kth smallest — it's the largest of the k smallest.

    Since Python only has min-heaps, I store negated values, which means negating on push and negating again when I read the top. Getting one of those two wrong inverts the whole comparison, so I'd comment it.

    Quickselect is the fastest on average — O(n) — because it's quicksort that only recurses into the side containing the answer. Partition puts the pivot at its final sorted position, so if that position equals k minus one, that element is the answer regardless of how unsorted the rest is. I'd randomise the pivot; without that, an already-sorted input degrades to O(n squared), which is a realistic input in practice. Downsides: it needs the whole array, it reorders it — so I'd copy first — and its worst case is quadratic.

    There's also a fourth: heapify the whole array in O(n) and pop k times, which is O(n plus k log n). That beats the size-k heap when k is very small.

    I'd guard k explicitly. Out-of-range k either throws an index error or silently returns a wrong answer depending on the approach, and silently wrong is worse."

    Problem 12.3 — K Closest Points To Origin¶

    Problem statement

    2D points ka array diya hai ([x, y] pairs) aur ek number k. Origin (0, 0) ke sabse nazdeek k points lauta do.

    Input:  points = [[1, 3], [-2, 2]], k = 1
Output: [[-2, 2]]
        distance([1,3]) = sqrt(1 + 9) = sqrt(10) = 3.16
        distance([-2,2]) = sqrt(4 + 4) = sqrt(8) = 2.83  <- closer

Input:  points = [[3, 3], [5, -1], [-2, 4]], k = 2
Output: [[3, 3], [-2, 4]]
        distances: sqrt(18) = 4.24, sqrt(26) = 5.10, sqrt(20) = 4.47

    Pehla instinct — brute force

    Har point ki distance nikaalo, sort karo, pehle k le lo.

    import math

def k_closest_sort(points, k):
    def distance(point):                          # 1: origin se distance
        x, y = point                              # 2
        return math.sqrt(x * x + y * y)           # 3: Euclidean distance

    points_sorted = sorted(points, key=distance)  # 4: distance par sort
    return points_sorted[:k]                      # 5: pehle k

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-3. Distance function. math.sqrt(x^2 + y^2) — Euclidean. 4. sorted(points, key=distance) — key function har element par ek baar chalta hai (Python ka "decorate-sort-undecorate" internally), toh n distance calculations. 5. points_sorted[:k] — pehle k. k > n par yeh poora list deta hai (crash nahi). k = 0 par khaali list — [:0] sahi behave karta hai (12.1 wale [-0:] bug se ulta).

    Complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n).

    Isme problem kya hai

    Do baatein:

    1. O(n log n) jab O(n log k) possible hai — wahi Problem 12.1 wali baat.
    2. math.sqrt bekaar hai — aur yeh ek chhota lekin real insight hai.

    The insight — do alag insights hain

    Insight 1 — square root mat nikaalo.

    Humein distances compare karni hain, unki actual values nahi chahiye. Aur sqrt ek monotonically increasing function hai:

    a < b  <=>  sqrt(a) < sqrt(b)     (a, b >= 0 ke liye)

    Toh x^2 + y^2 par compare karna aur sqrt(x^2 + y^2) par compare karna exactly same ordering deta hai.

    sqrt hataane ke teen fayde: - Faster — sqrt ek mehnga operation hai (hardware instruction lekin phir bhi multiplication se slow). - Exact — squared distance integer rehti hai (agar coordinates integers hain), toh koi floating-point precision issue nahi. sqrt float deta hai, aur do bahut kareeb distances float mein equal lag sakti hain. - Simpler — ek import kam.

    Yeh optimisation interview mein bolna bahut acha lagta hai kyunki yeh dikhata hai ki aap "problem kya maang rahi hai" aur "main kya compute kar raha hoon" mein farq dekh paate ho.

    Insight 2 — max-heap of size k.

    K closest chahiye, matlab k smallest distances. Toh max-heap (Problem 12.2 wali baat) — top par sabse door wala point, jise hataana hai.

    Optimal solution

    import heapq

def k_closest(points, k):
    if k <= 0:                                    # 1: guard
        return []                                 # 2

    heap = []                                     # 3: MAX-heap of (squared_distance, point)

    for x, y in points:                           # 4: unpack karke -- readable
        dist_sq = x * x + y * y                   # 5: NO sqrt -- ordering same rehti hai

        if len(heap) < k:                         # 6: heap abhi bhara nahi
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-dist_sq, x, y))# 7: NEGATE for max-heap
        elif dist_sq < -heap[0][0]:               # 8: naya point closer hai?
            heapq.heappushpop(heap, (-dist_sq, x, y))   # 9: swap

    return [[x, y] for _, x, y in heap]           # 10: tuples se lists banao

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. Guard. 3. heap = [] — max-heap of tuples. 4. for x, y in points: — unpacking se point[0], point[1] likhne se bach gaye. 5. dist_sq = x * x + y * y — koi sqrt nahi. x ** 2 bhi likh sakte the; x * x micro-faster hai aur equally clear. 6-7. heapq.heappush(heap, (-dist_sq, x, y)) — tuple mein teen elements. (-dist_sq, x, y) kyun, (-dist_sq, [x, y]) kyun nahi? Kyunki tuples lexicographically compare hote hain. Agar do points ki dist_sq same ho, toh Python dusre element par compare karega. Agar woh ek list hai ([x, y]) toh Python lists compare kar sakta hai (element-wise) — toh crash nahi hoga. Lekin agar woh ek custom object hota jismein __lt__ na ho, toh TypeError aata. (-dist_sq, x, y) mein sab integers hain — hamesha safe. Yeh Python heap ka classic gotcha hai aur interview mein mention karne layak. 8. elif dist_sq < -heap[0][0]: — -heap[0][0] = heap ka maximum squared distance. - heap[0] — top tuple. - heap[0][0] — uska pehla element (negated distance). - -heap[0][0] — actual distance. Do indices aur ek negation — yeh line galat likhna aasan hai. heap[0][0] ki jagah heap[0] likhne se tuple aur int compare hote hain → TypeError. 9. heappushpop — ek sift. 10. return [[x, y] for _, x, y in heap] — tuples se wapas lists. _ se pehla element (negated distance) discard kiya — hume woh output mein nahi chahiye. Output order heap ka internal order hai, sorted nahi. Problem usually order-agnostic hai — clarify karo.

    Quickselect version (agar O(n) average chahiye):

    import random

def k_closest_quickselect(points, k):
    points = list(points)                         # 11: copy
    n = len(points)                               # 12

    def dist_sq(p):                               # 13
        return p[0] * p[0] + p[1] * p[1]          # 14

    def partition(low, high):                     # 15
        rand = random.randint(low, high)          # 16: random pivot
        points[rand], points[high] = points[high], points[rand]   # 17
        pivot_dist = dist_sq(points[high])        # 18
        store = low                               # 19
        for i in range(low, high):                # 20
            if dist_sq(points[i]) < pivot_dist:   # 21
                points[store], points[i] = points[i], points[store]   # 22
                store += 1                        # 23
        points[store], points[high] = points[high], points[store]     # 24
        return store                              # 25

    low, high = 0, n - 1                          # 26
    while low <= high:                            # 27
        p = partition(low, high)                  # 28
        if p == k:                                # 29: pehle k elements final position par hain
            break                                 # 30
        elif p < k:                               # 31
            low = p + 1                           # 32
        else:                                     # 33
            high = p - 1                          # 34
    return points[:k]                             # 35

    Line 29 ka p == k (na ki k - 1) dhyaan se: hum k elements chahte hain, na ki kth element. Agar pivot index k par hai, toh indices 0..k-1 mein exactly k elements hain jo sab pivot se chhote hain — wahi answer hai.

    Time O(n) average, O(n^2) worst. Space O(1) (input copy ke alawa).

    Dry run — points = [[3, 3], [5, -1], [-2, 4]], k = 2

    Squared distances: [3,3] → 9+9 = 18. [5,-1] → 25+1 = 26. [-2,4] → 4+16 = 20.

    Step point dist_sq len(heap) < 2? heap max dist_sq < max? Action heap (actual dists)
    init — — — — — — {}
    1 [3,3] 18 0 < 2 Yes — — push {18}
    2 [5,-1] 26 1 < 2 Yes — — push {18, 26}
    3 [-2,4] 20 2 < 2 No -heap[0][0] = 26 20 < 26 Yes pushpop {18, 20}

    Heap mein {18, 20} → points [3,3] aur [-2,4]. Sahi.

    Step 3 ko dekho — 26 (sabse door) bahar gaya aur 20 andar. Heap ka top ab 20 hai.

    Aur note karo ki sqrt kahin nahi nikaali gayi — comparisons 18 < 26 aur 20 < 26 par hui, jo sqrt(18) < sqrt(26) ke barabar hai. Sahi answer, kam kaam.

    Dry run — precision ka concrete example

    Do points: [3, 4] (dist_sq = 25, dist = 5.0) aur [5, 0] (dist_sq = 25, dist = 5.0). Bilkul same distance.

    Squared version mein: 25 == 25 — tie. Tuple comparison (-25, 3, 4) vs (-25, 5, 0) → dusre element par compare → 3 < 5 → [3,4] "chhota" maana. Deterministic aur crash-free.

    Agar tuple (-25.0, [3,4]) hota (float distance aur list): -25.0 == -25.0 → list comparison → [3,4] < [5,0] → 3 < 5 → kaam kar jaata. Lekin agar point ek custom Point object hota toh TypeError.

    Aur ek asli precision case: coordinates 10^9 tak ho sakte hain. dist_sq = 2 * 10^18 — Python integer mein exact. math.sqrt(2 * 10**18) = 1414213562.3730950 — float, aur float ki precision 15-16 significant digits hai. Do points jinki squared distances 2*10^18 aur 2*10^18 + 1 hon, unke sqrt float mein equal ho sakte hain — galat ordering. Squared version exact hai.

    Complexity

    Approach Time Space
    Sort O(n log n) O(n)
    Max-heap size k O(n log k) O(k)
    Quickselect O(n) avg, O(n^2) worst O(1)

    Edge cases

    Case points k Output Kyun
    k = 0 [[1,1]] 0 [] Guard
    k > n [[1,1]] 5 [[1,1]] Heap kabhi bharta nahi
    k == n [[1,1],[2,2]] 2 dono
    Origin included [[0,0],[1,1]] 1 [[0,0]] dist_sq = 0
    All same distance [[1,0],[0,1],[-1,0]] 2 koi bhi 2 Tie-breaking arbitrary
    Negative coords [[-3,-4]] 1 [[-3,-4]] Squaring negatives handle karta
    Large coords [[10**9, 10**9]] 1 same Integer exact
    Empty [] 1 [] Loop chalta nahi

    "All same distance" wala row important hai — problem usually kehti hai "answer is guaranteed to be unique" ya "any valid answer". Clarify karo.

    Variations

    • K farthest points — min-heap (direction flip).
    • K closest to a given point (px, py) — dist_sq = (x-px)^2 + (y-py)^2.
    • Manhattan distance — abs(x) + abs(y); same structure.
    • K closest numbers to a target in a sorted array (LeetCode 658) — binary search plus two pointers, O(log n + k) — heap se better kyunki input sorted hai.
    • K closest in 3D — x^2 + y^2 + z^2.
    • Streaming points — yehi heap version, class ke roop mein.

    Interview answer: "Two things make this efficient, and the first one isn't about the heap at all.

    I never compute a square root. I only need to compare distances, and square root is monotonic on non-negative inputs, so comparing x-squared plus y-squared gives exactly the same ordering. That's faster, and more importantly it stays in exact integer arithmetic — with coordinates up to a billion, the squared distances reach two times ten to the eighteenth, and a float square root only carries about sixteen significant digits, so two genuinely different distances can compare equal. The squared version has no such problem.

    Second, a heap of size k rather than a full sort. Since I want the k closest, I keep a max-heap keyed on squared distance — the top is the farthest point I'm currently holding, which is exactly the one to evict when something closer arrives.

    One Python detail I'd flag: I push tuples of negated-distance, x, and y — three scalars — rather than negated-distance and the point object. Heap tuples are compared lexicographically, so when two distances tie Python falls through to the next element. With plain integers that's always fine; with a non-comparable object it raises a TypeError at an unpredictable moment, depending on whether a tie happens to occur in the data. Including a scalar tiebreaker makes it deterministic.

    O(n log k) time and O(k) space. If the whole array is in memory and I don't care about the order of the result, quickselect on squared distance gets O(n) average — partition until the pivot lands exactly at index k, then take the prefix — at the cost of mutating the array and an O(n squared) worst case, which I'd mitigate with a random pivot.

    I'd confirm whether ties matter — with several points at the same distance, which ones I return is arbitrary."

    Problem 12.4 — Connect Ropes For Minimum Cost¶

    Problem statement

    Alag alag lengths ki ropes di hain. Do ropes ko jodne ka cost = unki lengths ka sum. Saari ropes ko ek rope mein jodna hai. Minimum total cost kya hoga?

    Input:  ropes = [1, 3, 11, 5]
Output: 33

Best order: 1 + 3 = 4        (cost 4)
            4 + 5 = 9        (cost 9)
            9 + 11 = 20      (cost 20)
            Total = 4 + 9 + 20 = 33

Bura order: 11 + 5 = 16      (cost 16)
            16 + 3 = 19      (cost 19)
            19 + 1 = 20      (cost 20)
            Total = 16 + 19 + 20 = 55

Input:  ropes = [3, 4, 5, 6]
Output: 36

    Pehla instinct — brute force

    Har possible order try karo.

    def connect_ropes_brute(ropes):
    best = float('inf')                           # 1: minimum total cost

    def solve(remaining, cost_so_far):            # 2: `remaining` = bachi hui ropes
        nonlocal best                             # 3
        if len(remaining) == 1:                   # 4: ek hi rope bachi -- khatam
            best = min(best, cost_so_far)         # 5
            return                                # 6
        for i in range(len(remaining)):           # 7: har PAIR try karo
            for j in range(i + 1, len(remaining)):
                merged = remaining[i] + remaining[j]      # 8: joining cost
                rest = [remaining[x]                      # 9: naya list bina i, j ke
                        for x in range(len(remaining))
                        if x != i and x != j] + [merged]  # 10: plus merged rope
                solve(rest, cost_so_far + merged)         # 11: recurse

    solve(list(ropes), 0)                         # 12
    return best                                   # 13

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-3. Setup. nonlocal (Section 8 wali baat). 4-6. Base case: ek rope bachi. 7. Har pair try karo — C(n, 2) pairs har level par. 8. merged — joining cost. 9-10. Naya list banao bina i aur j ke, plus merged. O(n) per call. 11. Recurse with accumulated cost. 12-13.

    Complexity: Time bahut bura — har level par O(n^2) pairs aur n-1 levels. n = 10 par bhi slow. Space O(n^2).

    Isme problem kya hai

    Exponential. Aur asli baat: is problem mein ek clean greedy rule hai, toh saare orders try karne ki zaroorat hi nahi.

    The insight — aur yeh sabse important hissa hai

    Poocho: kaunsi ropes ka cost sabse zyada baar count hota hai?

    Jab aap do ropes jodte ho, unka combined length agli join mein bhi count hota hai, aur uske baad wali mein bhi. Yaani:

    Ek rope jitne "levels" tak carry hoti hai, uski length utni baar total cost mein add hoti hai.

    Example [1, 3, 11, 5] with best order: - 1 aur 3 pehle jude → dono 4 ka hissa bane → phir 9 ka → phir 20 ka. Dono teen baar counted. - 5 9 mein aayi → phir 20 mein. Do baar counted. - 11 sirf 20 mein aayi. Ek baar counted.

    Total = 1*3 + 3*3 + 5*2 + 11*1 = 3 + 9 + 10 + 11 = 33. Match.

    Toh rule saaf hai: badi ropes ko kam baar count karo, chhoti ropes ko zyada baar.

    Aur woh kaise? Hamesha do sabse chhoti ropes ko pehle jodo. Isse badi ropes late join hoti hain (kam levels).

    Yeh exactly Huffman coding ka algorithm hai — aur woh comparison interview mein bolna bahut strong hai. Huffman mein bhi frequently-occurring symbols ko chhote codes milte hain, aur mechanism bilkul yehi hai: min-heap se do sabse chhote nikaalo, jodo, wapas daalo.

    Optimal solution

    import heapq

def connect_ropes(ropes):
    if len(ropes) <= 1:                           # 1: 0 ya 1 rope -> koi joining nahi
        return 0                                  # 2: cost zero

    heap = list(ropes)                            # 3: copy -- caller ka array safe
    heapq.heapify(heap)                           # 4: MIN-heap, O(n)
    total_cost = 0                                # 5

    while len(heap) > 1:                          # 6: jab tak do ya zyada ropes hain
        first = heapq.heappop(heap)               # 7: sabse CHHOTI
        second = heapq.heappop(heap)              # 8: dusri sabse chhoti
        merged = first + second                   # 9: joining ka cost
        total_cost += merged                      # 10: total mein add
        heapq.heappush(heap, merged)              # 11: nayi rope WAPAS heap mein

    return total_cost                             # 12

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. <= 1 guard. Ek rope ko kisi se jodna nahi, toh cost 0. Guard technically optional hai (line 6 ka loop chalta hi nahi) lekin intent saaf karta hai. 3. heap = list(ropes) — copy. heapify in-place hai aur caller ka array reorder kar deta. 4. heapq.heapify(heap) — O(n), jabki n baar heappush O(n log n) hota. Yeh chhota optimisation mention karne layak hai. 5. total_cost = 0. 6. while len(heap) > 1: — > 1, > 0 nahi. Ek rope bachne par kuch jodna nahi hai. > 0 likhne se line 8 ka heappop khaali heap par → IndexError. 7-8. Do sabse chhoti ropes. 9. merged = first + second — joining cost. 10. total_cost += merged. 11. heapq.heappush(heap, merged) — nayi rope wapas heap mein. Yeh line hi algorithm ko "greedy with re-evaluation" banati hai. Nayi rope ab ek normal candidate hai aur shayad agli baar bhi sabse chhoti nikle. 12. Return.

    Loop kitni baar chalta hai: har iteration mein heap ka size exactly ek kam hota hai (do pop, ek push). n se 1 tak jaane mein n - 1 iterations — bilkul expected, kyunki n ropes ko jodne mein n-1 joins lagte hain.

    Greedy sahi kyun hai — exchange argument (interview mein bolne layak): Maan lo optimal solution mein do sabse chhoti ropes (a aur b) ek dusre ke saath pehle join nahi hoti. Toh unme se kam se kam ek kisi badi rope ke saath join hoti hai. Us join ko a-b join se replace karo — total cost badhta nahi, kyunki a + b kisi bhi dusre pair ke sum se chhota ya barabar hai. Toh ek optimal solution hamesha exist karta hai jismein do sabse chhoti pehle join hoti hain, aur recursion se poora greedy optimal ho jaata hai.

    Dry run — ropes = [1, 3, 11, 5] (expected 33)

    Iter heap (contents) first second merged total_cost heap (after)
    init {1, 3, 5, 11} — — — 0 —
    1 {1, 3, 5, 11} 1 3 1+3 = 4 4 {4, 5, 11}
    2 {4, 5, 11} 4 5 4+5 = 9 4+9 = 13 {9, 11}
    3 {9, 11} 9 11 9+11 = 20 13+20 = 33 {20}
    exit {20} — — — 33 len == 1 → stop

    Answer 33. Sahi.

    Iteration 2 sabse instructive hai — heap mein {4, 5, 11} the, aur 4 (jo abhi bana tha) sabse chhoti thi, toh woh phir se select hui. Yeh line 11 ka effect hai.

    Aur note karo ki 11 (sabse badi) sirf aakhri iteration mein use hui — exactly jaisa insight ne predict kiya tha. Uska contribution 11 * 1 = 11 hai, jabki 1 ka 1 * 3 = 3 hai.

    Dry run — ropes = [3, 4, 5, 6] (expected 36)

    Iter heap first second merged total_cost heap after
    1 {3,4,5,6} 3 4 7 7 {5, 6, 7}
    2 {5,6,7} 5 6 11 7+11 = 18 {7, 11}
    3 {7,11} 7 11 18 18+18 = 36 {18}

    Answer 36. Sahi.

    Level-counting se verify: 3 7 mein hai aur 7 18 mein hai → 3 do baar counted = 6. 4 bhi do baar = 8. 5 11 mein, 11 18 mein → do baar = 10. 6 bhi do baar = 12. Total 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 36. Match.

    Dry run — greedy vs non-greedy contrast — [1, 3, 11, 5] par bura order:

    Step Join Cost Running total
    1 11 + 5 = 16 16 16
    2 16 + 3 = 19 19 35
    3 19 + 1 = 20 20 55

    55 vs 33 — 67% zyada. Wajah saaf hai: 11 teen levels mein carry hui (11 * 3 = 33 contribution) jabki greedy mein sirf ek (11 * 1 = 11).

    Complexity

    • Time: O(n log n). heapify O(n), phir n - 1 iterations jinme do pops aur ek push (O(log n) each).
    • Space: O(n) heap ke liye.

    Kya sorting se ho sakta hai? Nahi — kyunki merged ropes ko wapas sorted order mein insert karna padta hai, aur sorted list mein insert O(n) hai. Heap O(log n) deta hai. Yeh explanation interview mein poochi jaati hai: "why not just sort once?"

    Edge cases

    Case ropes Output Kyun
    Empty [] 0 Guard
    Single [5] 0 Guard — koi joining nahi
    Two [3, 4] 7 Ek join
    All same [2,2,2,2] 16 4 + 4 + 8
    Sorted ascending [1,2,3,4] 19
    Sorted descending [4,3,2,1] 19 Same — heapify order normalise karta hai
    One huge [1,1,1000] 1004 1+1=2, 2+1000=1002 → 2 + 1002
    Zeros [0,0,5] 5 0+0=0, 0+5=5 → 0 + 5
    Large n 10^5 ropes — O(n log n) fine

    "Sorted descending" wala row important hai — input order bilkul matter nahi karta, kyunki heapify sab normalise kar deta hai.

    Variations

    • Huffman coding — bilkul yehi algorithm, lekin har merge par ek tree node banate hain aur tree return karte hain.
    • Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks (LeetCode 1167) — exactly yeh problem.
    • Maximum cost — max-heap use karo (do sabse badi jodo).
    • K ropes ek saath jod sakte ho — generalised Huffman; agar (n-1) % (k-1) != 0 toh dummy zeros add karne padte hain. Accha follow-up.
    • Ropes ko sirf adjacent hi jod sakte ho — greedy fail ho jaata hai, interval DP chahiye (Matrix Chain Multiplication family). Yeh distinction bolna bahut strong hai.
    • Har join ka cost max(a, b) ho — greedy shayad kaam na kare; case-by-case analysis chahiye.

    Interview answer: "The key question is: which ropes end up counted the most times? Every time two ropes merge, their combined length carries into the next merge, and the next. So a rope's length is added to the total once for every merge level it survives.

    That tells me the rule immediately: long ropes should participate in as few merges as possible, and short ones can afford to be counted many times. So I always merge the two shortest ropes available.

    A min-heap makes that a loop: pop the two smallest, add their sum to the running cost, push the sum back. The push-back matters — the merged rope is now an ordinary candidate and may well be the smallest again next iteration, which is exactly what happens in the example.

    Interviewers usually ask why I don't just sort once and merge in order. Because merged ropes have to re-enter the ordering, and inserting into a sorted list is O(n) while a heap insert is O(log n).

    For correctness, the exchange argument: if an optimal solution didn't merge the two smallest first, one of them merges with something larger — swapping that for the two-smallest merge never increases the total, since the two smallest have the smallest possible pair sum.

    This is Huffman coding, structurally identical.

    O(n log n) time — with an O(n) heapify up front rather than n pushes — and O(n) space.

    One useful contrast: if ropes could only merge with their neighbours, greedy breaks and it becomes an interval DP, the matrix-chain family. The freedom to merge any two is what makes greedy valid here."

    Problem 12.5 — Top K Frequent Elements¶

    Problem statement

    Array aur ek number k diya hai. K sabse frequent elements lauta do.

    Input:  nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2
Output: [1, 2]
        counts: {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1} -> top 2 by count = 1 aur 2

Input:  nums = [1], k = 1
Output: [1]

Input:  nums = [5, 12, 11, 5, 12, 12], k = 2
Output: [12, 5]
        counts: {5: 2, 12: 3, 11: 1}

    Pehla instinct — brute force

    Frequency count karo, phir counts par sort karo.

    from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent_sort(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)                        # 1: {value: frequency}, O(n)
    sorted_items = sorted(counts.items(),         # 2: (value, count) pairs
                          key=lambda item: item[1],   # 3: COUNT par sort
                          reverse=True)           # 4: descending
    return [value for value, _ in sorted_items[:k]]   # 5: top k ke values

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1. Counter(nums) — ek pass mein frequencies. O(n) time, O(d) space jahan d = distinct values. 2-4. sorted(counts.items(), key=..., reverse=True) — d items ko sort kiya, n nahi. key=lambda item: item[1] — tuple ka dusra element (count). reverse=True — sabse zyada frequent pehle.
    2. [value for value, _ in sorted_items[:k]] — values nikaalo, counts discard. _ convention se pata chalta hai ki count use nahi ho raha.

    Complexity: Time O(n + d log d) jahan d = distinct elements. Worst case d = n toh O(n log n). Space O(d).

    Ya Python built-in:

    def top_k_frequent_builtin(nums, k):
    return [v for v, _ in Counter(nums).most_common(k)]   # 6: ek line

    Line 6: Counter.most_common(k) internally heap use karta hai — O(n + d log k). Production mein yehi.

    Isme problem kya hai

    Sort wala version d distinct elements ko poori tarah order karta hai jab sirf k chahiye. Agar d = 10^6 aur k = 10 hai toh yeh waste hai.

    The insight — teen alag levels ke solutions

    Level 1 — heap of size k. Frequencies nikaalo, phir count par min-heap of size k rakho (top-K largest, toh min-heap — Problem 12.1 wali baat). O(n + d log k).

    Level 2 — bucket sort. Yeh sabse interesting hai.

    Observation: koi bhi frequency n se zyada nahi ho sakti. Toh frequencies ki range [1, n] hai — bounded.

    Toh ek array of buckets banao jahan buckets[f] = un saare values ki list jinki frequency f hai. Phir buckets ko peeche se aage traverse karo (highest frequency pehle) aur k values collect karo.

    Yeh O(n) hai — koi sorting nahi, koi heap nahi. Yeh bounded-range wala trick hai — bilkul wahi jo Cyclic Sort (Section 5) mein tha.

    Level 3 — quickselect on counts. O(d) average. Zyada complex, aur bucket sort already O(n) hai — toh usually zaroorat nahi.

    Optimal solution — heap version

    import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent_heap(nums, k):
    if k <= 0:                                    # 1: guard
        return []                                 # 2

    counts = Counter(nums)                        # 3: {value: frequency}

    heap = []                                     # 4: MIN-heap of (count, value)
    for value, count in counts.items():           # 5: har DISTINCT value
        if len(heap) < k:                         # 6: heap abhi bhara nahi
            heapq.heappush(heap, (count, value))  # 7: count PEHLE -- sorting key
        elif count > heap[0][0]:                  # 8: naya value top-k mein aata hai?
            heapq.heappushpop(heap, (count, value))   # 9

    return [value for _, value in heap]           # 10: values nikaalo

    Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

    1-2. Guard. 3. Counter(nums) — O(n). 4. heap = [] — min-heap (kyunki top-K largest counts chahiye). 5. for value, count in counts.items(): — d iterations, n nahi. Yeh already ek fayda hai. 6-7. heapq.heappush(heap, (count, value)) — (count, value) order zaroori hai. Tuples pehle element par compare hote hain, toh count pehle hona chahiye — wahi sorting key hai. (value, count) likhne se value par sort hota — bilkul galat.
